causeGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · Why these three causes
causeGuide.answer: The case itself says there is no clear learning path, and findings 1 to 3 show that learners cannot tell where to start or what comes next.
causeGuide.example: At LearnLoop the brief says new learners get no first-week guide, and two printed findings show long unexplained lists. Those are the causes I can point at; “the logo is old” has nothing printed behind it.
causeGuide.why: A cause is defended by a printed fact. The plan's model solution names the main problem as a lack of structure and orientation.
lookFor: Points at a printed finding or a case line.
Does not offer a cause the case never mentions.

decisionOrderGuide.title: 3.1 · Why the first decision goes first (Core)
decisionOrderGuide.answer: Paths come first because every learner meets orientation before anything else. Progress is cheap and builds on the path. Research runs alongside so later decisions rest on what learners actually do.
decisionOrderGuide.example: The guided start comes first because it meets every new learner, and it gives the later decisions a baseline to be measured against.
decisionOrderGuide.why: The roadmap is an order with a reason. The model order is paths, progress, research; a different order defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one.
Refers to reach, cost, dependency or evidence.

giveUpGuide.title: 3.2 · What you give up or postpone (Core)
giveUpGuide.answer: I give up the badge system and the AI recommendations for this year, and I postpone rewriting the ten longest lessons; learners will keep the long lessons for now.
giveUpGuide.example: I give up the leaderboard this year, and I postpone the full catalogue rewrite; learners keep the old lesson texts for now.
giveUpGuide.why: The skill of Level 3: a decision that gives up nothing has not decided. The answer names something real that a stakeholder would miss.
lookFor: Names a concrete thing given up or postponed.
It is something someone would miss, not a throwaway.

missingGuide.title: 2.2 · What information you are missing (Core)
missingGuide.answer: I do not know why the 40 learners leave: the findings show what is hard, not what makes a learner decide to stop. I would interview ten who left before spending all of the €50,000.
missingGuide.example: I do not know whether week-one leavers lack direction or lack time. I would run five short interviews before committing the whole €30,000.
missingGuide.why: The plan asks it outright (“Welche Information fehlt Ihnen?”). The good answer names an unknown that would change the decision, and a way to find it out.
lookFor: Names a specific unknown, not “more data”.
Says how it could be found out.
Connects to the decision (what would change).

needGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · What you would need to find out why learners leave
needGuide.answer: I would interview some of the 40 who left and look at the lesson where most of them stop, because the number only says that they left, not why.
needGuide.example: I would not guess from the 30% alone. I would ask ten learners who left in week one what they were trying to do when they stopped.
needGuide.why: The trap the app reveals: the number counts who left, not why. A good answer names a source that could show why (interviews, a usability test, data per lesson), not a measure.
lookFor: Names at least one source of evidence about the learners themselves.
Does not turn the number into a cause.

orderGuide.title: 2.2 · Why the first priority goes first (Core)
orderGuide.answer: Learning paths come first because every learner meets the orientation problem before anything else, and the other three measures work better once a path exists.
orderGuide.example: At LearnLoop the guided first week goes first: week one is where learners leave, and at €7,000 it is cheap enough to start before anything else.
orderGuide.why: The plan's model solution puts learning paths first (“greatest impact”). A different first priority defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Refers to the learner's problem, the cost or what the others depend on.

reflectGuide.title: 1.3 (Optional) · Coaching reflection
reflectGuide.answer: Showing learners where they are and what comes next improves learning more than any new feature, because without it they never reach the content. Critical: a clear path and visible progress. Nice to have: a new look or extra courses. Completion: a clear path lets learners finish, and finishing is what the platform earns from.
reflectGuide.why: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: UX is not a design problem but a decision problem; designing beautifully against designing effectively; thinking in user flows instead of single screens. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.

riskPlanGuide.title: 3.2 · What you do about the biggest risk (Core)
riskPlanGuide.answer: I fund the research programme next to the fixes, so that we find out why learners leave and can correct course after the first quarter.
riskPlanGuide.example: I reserve part of the budget for interviews in the first month, so that if the guided start misses the real cause, we find out before the second decision.
riskPlanGuide.why: A risk with no action is only a worry. The action should be concrete: what is done, and when it is checked.
lookFor: Names an action.
Says when or how the risk would be noticed.

uncertainGuide.title: 3.2 · The decision without complete data (Core)
uncertainGuide.answer: I decide to build learning paths for the three most-taken courses now. I do not know whether learners leave from lack of direction or from lack of time. I will refocus if, after the first quarter, the drop-out in those courses has not fallen from 40% to below 35%.
uncertainGuide.example: I decide to launch a guided first week now. I do not know whether leavers lack direction or time. I will reverse and test a shorter format if week-one drop-out has not fallen from 30% to below 25% after six weeks.
uncertainGuide.why: The frame of Materi B3: what I decide, what I do not know, what would make me reverse and by when. A checkable reversal condition has a figure and a date.
lookFor: States the decision.
States what is not known.
Gives a checkable reversal condition with a figure and a time.
pitfalls: A decision with no stated unknown (“we will improve UX”).
A reversal condition no one could check (“if it does not work”).

visionGuide.title: 3.1 · The UX vision (Core)
visionGuide.answer: Learning at SkillUp should feel guided and visible: every learner always knows where they are, what comes next and how far they have come.
visionGuide.example: Learning at LearnLoop should feel like a clear first week and a visible next step, so a busy professional never wonders what to do now.
visionGuide.why: The plan's question: “Wie soll Lernen erlebt werden?”. A good vision describes the learner's experience, not a feature list.
lookFor: Describes how learning feels or what the learner can do.
One or two sentences.
Is not a list of features or a business target alone.

worstGuide.title: 1.1 · The finding that would make a learner give up first (Core)
worstGuide.answer: On my first visit I see 14 identical tiles and nothing that says what to do first. I would not know where to begin, and I would leave before I had even started a lesson.
worstGuide.example: At LearnLoop a new learner sees a list of 20 courses and no suggestion. I would pick none and close the tab: I came to learn something specific, and nothing tells me which course is mine.
worstGuide.why: Any of the eight findings defends. What the plan asks for is the user's perspective (“Versetzen Sie sich in einen Lernenden”): the reason must say what the learner cannot do or feel, not that something looks wrong.
lookFor: Written from the learner's side (“I would not know…”), not about the design.
Names a concrete consequence (leaving, getting lost, giving up).
Refers to the finding chosen, not to the platform in general.

architectureKey.title: Block 3.2 · Who decides, on what evidence
architectureKey.expected: Who: The UX lead together with the product owner. Evidence: Learner interviews; A usability test of the new screens; Drop-out data per lesson.

options.label: Who decides: The Chief UX Officer alone
options.why: Defendable, but one person's taste is exactly what a decision architecture should prevent.

options.label: Who decides: The UX lead together with the product owner
options.why: UX judgement and product ownership together: neither taste alone nor build convenience.

options.label: Who decides: A steering group with management
options.why: Defendable for large budget items; too slow for routine UX decisions.

options.label: Who decides: Whoever builds the feature
options.why: Rejected: the builder decides what is easy to build, not what learners need.

options.label: Evidence: Learner interviews
options.why: Evidence from learners themselves.

options.label: Evidence: A usability test of the new screens
options.why: Evidence from learners themselves.

options.label: Evidence: Drop-out data per lesson
options.why: Evidence from learners themselves.

options.label: Evidence: A comparison with competitors
options.why: Useful context, not evidence about SkillUp's own learners.

options.label: Evidence: The opinion of the most senior person in the room
options.why: Rejected: authority is not evidence.

architectureKey.teachingNote: At least two kinds of evidence are required; the sort of evidence a learner chooses is judged on the reason in the memo, not on matching the model.

causeKey.title: Block 2.1 (Optional) · Three main causes
causeKey.expected: Learners have no clear path through a course: what to do first, next and last.  |  Lessons are hard to follow: long, unstructured text with unexplained terms.  |  Learners cannot see their progress or whether they are succeeding.

options.label: Learners have no clear path through a course: what to do first, next and last.
options.why: The case names it (“no clear learning path”), and findings 1 to 3 show it.

options.label: Lessons are hard to follow: long, unstructured text with unexplained terms.
options.why: The case names it (“content hard to understand”), and findings 4 to 6 show it.

options.label: Learners cannot see their progress or whether they are succeeding.
options.why: Findings 7 and 8 show it (no progress bar, no message after a quiz).

options.label: The visual style of the platform looks dated.
options.why: No printed finding says so; it is about the surface, not the experience.

options.label: The course catalogue is too small.
options.why: Nothing in the case says learners leave for lack of courses.

options.label: The subscription price is too high.
options.why: The case mentions no price complaint.

causeKey.teachingNote: The plan's model solution names the main problem as a lack of structure and orientation. A learner who swaps one cause for another and points at a printed fact (a finding or a case line) defends the choice; a cause with no printed evidence does not.

claimKey.title: Block 1.2 (Optional) · What the 40% shows and does not show
claimKey.expected: 40 of every 100 learners who start a course do not finish it. → the number shows this  |  Learners leave because the lessons are too hard. → the number does not show this  |  A progress bar would bring the number down. → the number does not show this  |  More than one in three learners who start do not finish. → the number shows this  |  The 40 who leave are the learners who find the content boring. → the number does not show this

options.label: 40 of every 100 learners who start a course do not finish it.
options.why: It only restates the number.

options.label: Learners leave because the lessons are too hard.
options.why: A drop-out rate counts who left, not why.

options.label: A progress bar would bring the number down.
options.why: A number does not predict the effect of a measure.

options.label: More than one in three learners who start do not finish.
options.why: 40 of 100 is more than a third (about 33).

options.label: The 40 who leave are the learners who find the content boring.
options.why: It says nothing about feelings or reasons.

claimKey.teachingNote: The trap the app reveals: a rate counts who left, never why. Anyone who ticks “shows” for a reason or a remedy has read a cause into a symptom. This is the coaching point of the plan (“Daten zeigen Symptome, nicht Ursachen” appears on Day 16; on Day 1 the equivalent is “dealing with incomplete user information”).

decisionKey.title: Block 3.1 · Three strategic decisions
decisionKey.expected: Guided learning paths for the three most-taken courses; Progress and feedback on every course page and quiz; A standing user-research programme

options.label: Guided learning paths for the three most-taken courses
options.why: Reference pick: €45,000, 16 weeks. It meets a printed finding that every learner meets.

options.label: Progress and feedback on every course page and quiz
options.why: Reference pick: €25,000, 12 weeks. It meets a printed finding that every learner meets.

options.label: Rewrite the ten longest lessons as short, structured units
options.why: Defendable: it meets the Understanding finding, but at €40,000 and 20 weeks it is the costliest fix; it would go next year.

options.label: A standing user-research programme
options.why: Reference pick: €30,000, 52 weeks. It is the decision that lets later decisions rest on evidence, which the decision-architecture item of the plan asks for.

options.label: Points, badges and a leaderboard
options.why: Rejected in the plan's own logic: extrinsic reward, answers no printed finding, and the effect fades; competitors using it is not a reason.

options.label: AI-driven personal recommendations
options.why: Rejected: €90,000 is most of the budget, it needs data SkillUp does not have, and learners cannot see why they are shown what they see.

options.label: Double the marketing budget
options.why: Rejected: it fixes acquisition, not experience; more learners arriving at the same platform leave at the same rate.

decisionKey.teachingNote: A different set of three defends if the reason is written and the three together answer the vision. Budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38); a set over the €120,000 limit exports with the amount printed as a fact.

measureKey.title: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
measureKey.expected: Define learning paths; Split lessons into short units; Add a progress indicator; Structure the text of each lesson. Total €47,000 of €50,000.

options.label: Define learning paths
options.why: Answers a printed finding (orientation). Effort High by the printed cost €18,000. Reference ratings: user impact High, risk Mid.

options.label: Split lessons into short units
options.why: Answers a printed finding (understanding). Effort Mid by the printed cost €14,000. Reference ratings: user impact Mid, risk Mid.

options.label: Add a progress indicator
options.why: Answers a printed finding (motivation). Effort Low by the printed cost €6,000. Reference ratings: user impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: Structure the text of each lesson
options.why: Answers a printed finding (understanding). Effort Low by the printed cost €9,000. Reference ratings: user impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: Points and badges
options.why: Rejected in the plan's own logic: points and badges are extrinsic and answer none of the three findings areas directly; the short-term effect fades and the cost is Mid. A learner who funds it must say what it does for the learner.

options.label: Discussion forum
options.why: Rejected: a new feature, tied to no printed finding, and the most expensive option (€22,000, effort High).

options.label: New visual style
options.why: Rejected: it changes the look (UI), not the experience; no printed finding is about the look.

options.label: Ten new courses
options.why: Rejected: more content serves a business goal, not a learner's problem; €20,000 for effort High.

options.label: Interview learners who left, and test one course
options.why: Defendable, not in the model: it gathers evidence (cost €7,000, effort Low) and answers the “what information are you missing” item. A learner who funds it instead of m4 should say which measure they drop and why.

measureKey.teachingNote: Effort is rule-based (under €10,000 Low, up to €15,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; user impact and risk are judgements and are never marked. A different, well-reasoned choice is acceptable and exports (CLAUDE.md #38): over budget, another set of four, a different order, all with a stated reason. The plan's model solution orders them: learning paths (greatest impact), modular content, progress indicator, less cognitive load; its rationale line “Impact > Effort > User impact” is read here as: impact first, then what it costs.

riskKey.title: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk
riskKey.expected: We treat the symptom (drop-out) and miss its cause.

options.label: We treat the symptom (drop-out) and miss its cause.
options.why: The central risk of the whole plan: SkillUp knows what is hard on the screens, not why learners stop. The research programme is the answer to it.

options.label: Competitors improve faster than we do while we prepare.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the cause-versus-symptom risk because the plan's own coaching names it (“UX is not a design problem but a decision problem”).

options.label: Learners do not use the new paths or progress views.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the cause-versus-symptom risk because the plan's own coaching names it (“UX is not a design problem but a decision problem”).

options.label: The budget is used up before a first result is visible.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the cause-versus-symptom risk because the plan's own coaching names it (“UX is not a design problem but a decision problem”).

options.label: Management expects the drop-out rate to fall within weeks.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the cause-versus-symptom risk because the plan's own coaching names it (“UX is not a design problem but a decision problem”).

riskKey.teachingNote: Any of the five defends when the plan to meet it is concrete (what is done, by whom, when). The wrong answer is a risk with no action.

sortKey.title: Block 1.1 · Eight findings into Orientation, Understanding, Motivation
sortKey.expected: Orientation: 14 equal tiles on the dashboard; Yesterday's course is four clicks away; No “Next lesson” button  |  Understanding: One 500-word block of text; Technical terms without explanation; Very long sentences  |  Motivation: No progress bar; No message after a quiz

options.label: 14 equal tiles on the dashboard
options.why: Orientation. The learner cannot tell where to start: orientation.

options.label: Yesterday's course is four clicks away
options.why: Orientation. The learner cannot find where they stopped: orientation.

options.label: No “Next lesson” button
options.why: Orientation. The learner is not told what comes next: orientation.

options.label: One 500-word block of text
options.why: Understanding. The learner has to dig the structure out of the text themselves: understanding.

options.label: Technical terms without explanation
options.why: Understanding. The learner stops at words they do not know: understanding.

options.label: Very long sentences
options.why: Understanding. Long sentences cost attention that is then missing for learning: understanding.

options.label: No progress bar
options.why: Motivation. The learner cannot see they are getting somewhere: motivation, through progress.

options.label: No message after a quiz
options.why: Motivation. The learner gets no sign of success or failure: motivation, through feedback.

sortKey.teachingNote: The sort is objective: each finding breaks one of the three questions taught in Materi A3. Some findings touch two areas (a wall of text also hides where the main point is); the test is which question the printed phrase breaks first. The 40% drop-out figure is deliberately not a finding to sort: it is where the three areas end up. The second part of the block (the one finding that would make a learner give up first) is judged: any of the eight defends if the reason is written from the learner's side. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, categories Orientation, Understanding, Motivation.

adaptiveGuide.title: 2.2 · The decision on adaptive learning (Core)
adaptiveGuide.answer: Partly: first fix path and feedback with low-fidelity tests, then try one rule-based step, a pre-test that lets learners skip what they know, in one course. The algorithmic part waits for data and the legal check.
adaptiveGuide.example: For a platform with little data and one clear problem, I would say “partly”: start with one rule, a pre-test that lets learners skip the basics, and wait with an algorithm until there are enough learners and the legal check is done.
adaptiveGuide.why: The plan's model solution introduces adaptive elements only step by step. The three questions of Materi A5: is there a learner problem that individual paths solve, is there enough data, are there content variants? “Partly” is a real answer.
lookFor: Says yes, partly or no and gives a reason.
Names the first step.
If partly, says which part waits.

approachGuide.title: 2.2 · Why this prototype approach (Core)
approachGuide.answer: It answers the first question, whether learners can complete a whole course flow, with a clickable low-fidelity version, so a mistake in structure is cheap to fix. It leaves the final look and the speed of the real platform for later.
approachGuide.example: For LearnLoop I would pick the clickable grey-box version of the course start: it answers “can learners find the next step?” first, and it leaves the colours and the final speed for a later round.
approachGuide.why: The plan's model solution: low-fidelity tests first, focus on learning paths and interaction. A good answer names the question the approach answers first and what it leaves for later.
lookFor: Names the first question the approach answers.
Says what it leaves for later.
Does not choose polish or a full build while needs are unclear.

giveUpGuide.title: 3.2 · What you give up or postpone (Core)
giveUpGuide.answer: I give up the AI recommendation engine this year, and I postpone the new visual design; learners keep the current look for now.
giveUpGuide.example: I give up the personal-recommendation engine this year, and I postpone the new visual style; learners keep the current look for now.
giveUpGuide.why: The skill of Level 3: a decision that gives up nothing has not decided. The answer names something real that a stakeholder would miss.
lookFor: Names a concrete thing given up or postponed.
It is something someone would miss, not a throwaway.

invOrderGuide.title: 3.1 · Why the first investment goes first (Core)
invOrderGuide.answer: The guided path and feedback redesign goes first: it reaches every learner, costs little and is tested with prototypes before it is built. The dashboard follows, because the pilot needs data to be read, and the pilot comes last since it depends on both.
invOrderGuide.example: The guided start comes first because it reaches every new learner and is tested on paper before it is built; the analytics come second because the pilot needs them.
invOrderGuide.why: The roadmap is an order with a reason. The model order is path and feedback, then data, then the pilot; a different order defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one.
Refers to reach, cost, dependency or evidence.

missingGuide.title: 2.2 · What information you are missing (Core)
missingGuide.answer: I do not know why learners leave: the drop-out data would show where, not why. I would interview eight learners who left before choosing what to build.
missingGuide.example: I do not know whether learners leave because the start is confusing or because the course is too long. I would interview six who left before choosing what to build.
missingGuide.why: The plan's brief says user needs are unclear. A good answer names a specific unknown that would change the decision, and a way to find it out.
lookFor: Names a specific unknown, not “more data”.
Says how it could be found out.
Connects to the decision (what would change).

optRiskGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · The risk that worries you most without testing
optRiskGuide.answer: The one that worries me most is that we find out late: a change after the build costs far more than a change on paper.
optRiskGuide.example: What worries me most is that learners leave before we know why: we would only see the number fall, never the reason.
optRiskGuide.why: Not scored. The point is to name a risk of the case in the learner's own words.
lookFor: Names a risk that applies to the case.
Says why it matters to this team.

optWhyGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · Your decision under time pressure
optWhyGuide.answer: Option B costs €6,500 and takes two weeks, and afterwards we know what works. A is polished but built on an untested idea, and C finds problems only when learners leave.
optWhyGuide.example: I would test low-fidelity first: it costs a fraction of the budget, and after two weeks we know what learners do, which the other two options cannot tell us before the money is spent.
optWhyGuide.why: The plan's rationale: minimise risk before maximising technology. A good answer refers to the cost, to what will be known afterwards, or to what could go wrong.
lookFor: Gives a reason in terms of cost, evidence gained or risk.
Does not rest on “it looks finished”.

preferGuide.title: 1.1 · Which platform you would prefer, and why (Core)
preferGuide.answer: On Platform A I always see the next step and how far I have come, so I can fit a unit into ten minutes and know when I am done. On Platform B I would scroll for forty minutes with no sign of progress, and I would stop.
preferGuide.example: On the platform I would prefer, a unit is marked “8 min” and the next one waits at the bottom, so I can use a coffee break. On the other I could not tell how long anything would take, and I would put it off.
preferGuide.why: Either platform defends, but the plan asks for the preference with a reason (“welche Plattform würden Sie bevorzugen und warum?”). The reason must say what the learner can do or feel, not that one looks nicer.
lookFor: Written from the learner's side (“I can…”, “I would…”).
Names something the learner can do or see on one platform and not on the other.
Is not only “it looks nicer”.

principleGuide.title: 1.1 · Three principles of success, “Do X, because Y” (Core)
principleGuide.answer: Show the learner the next step, because a learner who has to search for it may stop before they find it. Cut the content into units of a few minutes with one goal each, because a learner with ten free minutes can only start what they can finish. Show progress and give a result after every task, because without a sign of success the effort feels wasted.
principleGuide.example: Name the goal of every unit at the top, because a learner who knows what a unit is for can tell whether it is worth ten minutes.
principleGuide.why: The plan asks to derive three principles of success from the differences. A good principle is a sentence with a reason, tied to one of the three practices (path, short units, feedback), not a feature name.
lookFor: Each principle has “Do X” and “because Y”.
The three are different (not the same idea three times).
Each can be traced to a difference between the two platforms.
pitfalls: A feature name with no reason (“a progress bar”).
A result listed as a principle (“completion rises”).

prototypingGuide.title: 3.1 · Prototyping strategy (Core)
prototypingGuide.answer: We start with low-fidelity: paper and clickable prototypes with five learners per round. The first question is whether learners can find the next step and finish a unit, before anything is built.
prototypingGuide.example: We test every new feature on paper first with five learners, and move to a clickable version only when the first question, whether learners find the next step, is answered.
prototypingGuide.why: Materi A2: choose the fidelity by the question; test low-fidelity first when needs are unclear.
lookFor: Names the fidelity to start with.
Names the first question it answers.
Says how many users or rounds (about five per group).

r2AdaptiveGuide.title: 3.1 · Do we invest in adaptive learning? (Core)
r2AdaptiveGuide.answer: Partly: I fund one small, tested step now, a guided path with feedback and a rule-based pilot in one course, and the recommendation engine waits until the pilot shows a result and our data and legal checks are in place.
r2AdaptiveGuide.example: I would say “partly”: fund a rule-based pilot in one course now, with a control group, and let the AI engine wait for the gate that checks the pilot's result.
r2AdaptiveGuide.why: The plan asks yes, no or partly. Materi B1: treat the investment as a staged bet; “partly” means the part the evidence supports now, and the rest waits for its gate.
lookFor: States yes, partly or no.
If partly, says what is funded now and what waits.
Does not follow competitors as the only reason.

reflectGuide.title: 1.3 (Optional) · Coaching reflection
reflectGuide.answer: We build the wrong thing and find out when learners leave, when change is expensive. The decision to build before testing: everything after it is rework. Technology makes sense when a learner problem needs it and simpler measures fall short; otherwise it is over-engineering.
reflectGuide.why: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: successful platforms are not “good by chance”; prototyping reduces risk; testing is the basis for decisions. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.

riskPlanGuide.title: 3.2 · What you do about the biggest risk (Core)
riskPlanGuide.answer: I put the dashboard and the consent basis before the pilot, so that nothing is built that the data cannot support. I would notice the risk if the pilot cannot be measured in the first month.
riskPlanGuide.example: I reserve the first month for a consent and data check, so that if the data cannot support the pilot, we know before we spend on it.
riskPlanGuide.why: A risk with no action is only a worry. The action should be concrete: what is done, and when it is noticed.
lookFor: Names an action.
Says when or how the risk would be noticed.

testQGuide.title: 2.2 · The question each chosen test answers (Core)
testQGuide.answer: Do learners complete the whole flow of the clickable prototype, and where do they hesitate? At which lesson do learners leave today? It shows where, so we know where to look. Why did learners who left stop? It is the only test here that can show the reason.
testQGuide.example: A drop-out count per lesson shows where learners leave. It does not show why, so it is paired with a test where I can watch five learners try the first lesson.
testQGuide.why: A test is chosen for the question it answers. A set that only counts (all quantitative) or only watches (all qualitative) leaves half of the question open: where, and why.
lookFor: States a question, not the name of the test again.
Matches the kind of data the test gives (why or how many).
Does not claim a test shows what it cannot (a count does not show a cause).
pitfalls: Three tests of the same kind.
Choosing the usability test of the full high-fidelity redesign before the design exists.

uncertainGuide.title: 3.2 · The decision under uncertainty (Core)
uncertainGuide.answer: I decide to run a rule-based personalisation pilot in one course. I do not know whether learners want recommended steps or whether our data is good enough. I will reverse it if pilot completion is not at least five points above the control group after eight weeks.
uncertainGuide.example: I decide to run a pre-test pilot in one course. I do not know whether our learners will skip basics they think they know. I will reverse it if fewer than 60% of those who skip pass the later quiz after six weeks.
uncertainGuide.why: The frame of Materi B3: what I decide, what I do not know, what would make me reverse and by when. A checkable reversal condition has a figure and a time.
lookFor: States the decision.
States what is not known.
Gives a checkable reversal condition with a figure and a time.
pitfalls: A reversal condition no one could check (“if it does not work”).
A decision that gives up an irreversible commitment instead of a pilot.

weakGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · Which printed fact supports your first weakness
weakGuide.answer: Facts 7 and 8 show the feedback weakness: no sign of progress and no message after the last page. The case itself says there is no personalisation and that the content is rated boring.
weakGuide.example: At LearnLoop the brief says new learners get no first-week guide, and two printed facts show long unexplained lists. Those are the weaknesses I can point at; “the logo is old” has nothing printed behind it.
weakGuide.why: A weakness is defended by a printed fact. The plan's model solution names the main problem as a lack of feedback and individualisation.
lookFor: Points at a printed fact (by its number) or quotes a case line.
Does not offer a weakness the case never mentions.

adaptiveKey.title: Block 2.2 and 3.1 · Is adaptive learning worthwhile? Yes, partly or no

options.label: Yes
options.why: Defendable only with a reason that names the learner problem, the data and the legal check; a plain “yes” because competitors have it is the hype the plan warns against.

options.label: Partly
options.why: Reference answer, the plan's “only step by step”: one simple, tested step (a rule, in one course) now, and the algorithmic part waits for data, content variants and the legal check.

options.label: No
options.why: Defendable if the reason is that the data and the content variants are not there; but “no” without a first step ignores the plan's complaint of no personalisation.

adaptiveKey.teachingNote: The three questions of Materi A5: is there a learner problem that individual paths solve, is there enough data of good quality, are there content variants to adapt to? Without them it is over-engineering. “Partly” is a real answer when it says which part is funded and which waits.

approachKey.title: Block 2.2 · The prototype approach
approachKey.expected: P2 · A clickable low-fidelity prototype of the whole course flow (start, unit, quiz, end); test; refine (€14,000, 5 weeks)

options.label: P1 · Paper sketches of the course start and the learning path; test with five learners; then a clickable low-fidelity version (€5,000, 2 weeks)
options.why: Defendable and the cheapest start: it answers “can learners find the next step?” first. It tests only the start of the course, so the quiz and the end are left for a second round; the answer should say so.

options.label: P2 · A clickable low-fidelity prototype of the whole course flow (start, unit, quiz, end); test; refine (€14,000, 5 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: a clickable low-fidelity version of the whole flow tests structure, order and wording end to end, cheaply, and leaves the look for later.

options.label: P3 · A high-fidelity prototype of the whole platform with the final look (€36,000, 8 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: polish before the idea is tested; €36,000 and 8 weeks for what a rough version would show, and a team that defends a good-looking prototype.

options.label: P4 · Build the adaptive engine first and test it on the real platform (€72,000, 14 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: €72,000 is over the €60,000 budget and 14 weeks is over the 12-week limit; it builds technology before knowing the problem, and it needs data the platform does not have.

options.label: P5 · Build the redesign directly and test after launch (€54,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: no test before launch; problems are found by learners who leave, and the budget goes into rework.

approachKey.teachingNote: The plan's model solution: low-fidelity tests first, focus on learning paths and interaction. P1 and P2 both fit; the answer to “why” must name the question it answers first and what it leaves for later. A choice over the budget or the time exports with the amount printed as a fact (CLAUDE.md #38).

architectureKey.title: Block 3.2 · Who decides, on what evidence
architectureKey.expected: Who: The product lead together with the head of data. Evidence: A pilot with a control group; A usability test of the new screens; Drop-out data per lesson.

options.label: Who decides: The Chief Product Officer alone
options.why: Defendable, but one person's taste is exactly what a decision rule should prevent.

options.label: Who decides: The product lead together with the head of data
options.why: Product judgement and data together: neither taste alone nor a sales story.

options.label: Who decides: A steering group with management
options.why: Defendable for large budget items; too slow for routine decisions.

options.label: Who decides: The vendor of the technology
options.why: Rejected: the vendor decides what it can sell, not what LearnPro's learners need.

options.label: Evidence: A pilot with a control group
options.why: Evidence from LearnPro's own learners.

options.label: Evidence: A usability test of the new screens
options.why: Evidence from LearnPro's own learners.

options.label: Evidence: Drop-out data per lesson
options.why: Evidence from LearnPro's own learners.

options.label: Evidence: A vendor demonstration or competitor comparison
options.why: Useful context, not evidence about LearnPro's own learners.

options.label: Evidence: The opinion of the most senior person in the room
options.why: Rejected: authority is not evidence.

architectureKey.teachingNote: At least two kinds of evidence are required; the sort of evidence a learner chooses is judged on the reason in the memo, not on matching the model.

dataKey.title: Block 3.1 · Which data the testing strategy needs
dataKey.expected: Drop-out per lesson from existing logs (shows where learners leave)  |  Interviews with learners who left (shows why)  |  Completion per course in a pilot with a control group  |  Consent and legal basis for tracking learners

options.label: Drop-out per lesson from existing logs (shows where learners leave)
options.why: Evidence about LearnPro's own learners that answers where, why, or whether a change worked; the consent line is the legal basis for tracking.

options.label: Interviews with learners who left (shows why)
options.why: Evidence about LearnPro's own learners that answers where, why, or whether a change worked; the consent line is the legal basis for tracking.

options.label: Task success and time in usability tests
options.why: Defendable when the learner can say which question it answers (task success and time answer “can they do it”; time on task in the live platform needs consent and a purpose).

options.label: Completion per course in a pilot with a control group
options.why: Evidence about LearnPro's own learners that answers where, why, or whether a change worked; the consent line is the legal basis for tracking.

options.label: Time on task in the live platform
options.why: Defendable when the learner can say which question it answers (task success and time answer “can they do it”; time on task in the live platform needs consent and a purpose).

options.label: Competitors' feature lists
options.why: Rejected: a competitor's feature list is context, not evidence about LearnPro's learners.

options.label: Consent and legal basis for tracking learners
options.why: Evidence about LearnPro's own learners that answers where, why, or whether a change worked; the consent line is the legal basis for tracking.

dataKey.teachingNote: At least three are required; which ones is judged on the question each answers, not on matching the model.

invKey.title: Block 3.1 · Three investments for the roadmap
invKey.expected: Guided path and feedback redesign, tested with low-fidelity prototypes; Learning-analytics dashboard for the product team; Rule-based personalisation pilot

options.label: I1 · Guided path and feedback redesign, tested with low-fidelity prototypes (€30,000, 10 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it meets the feedback and path weaknesses, is tested with prototypes before building, and reaches every learner.

options.label: I2 · Rule-based personalisation pilot (€40,000, 16 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: one small adaptive step with a control group; this is what “partly” means in money.

options.label: I3 · Learning-analytics dashboard for the product team (€25,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: the data foundation, with consent and a purpose, that the pilot and every later decision need (Materi B1: check the data foundation before the technology).

options.label: I4 · A standing prototype-and-test routine (€20,000, 52 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: a standing routine that makes every later feature cheaper to test; it runs 52 weeks, so the result is slow.

options.label: I5 · AI recommendation engine for all courses (€120,000, 40 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: €120,000 is most of the budget, it needs data the platform does not record, and learners could not see why they are shown what they see.

options.label: I6 · New visual design of the whole platform (€60,000, 20 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: it changes the look, not the experience; no printed finding is about the look.

options.label: I7 · Interactive exercises for the three most boring courses (€45,000, 20 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: it meets the “boring” complaint, but without feedback and a path the new exercises sit inside the same confusing structure.

invKey.teachingNote: A different set of three defends if the reason is written and the three together answer the plan. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38); a set over the €200,000 limit exports with the amount printed as a fact.

optKey.title: Block 1.2 (Optional) · Prototyping and testing under time pressure
optKey.expected: Decision: Test low-fidelity first. Effort by the printed cost: A Mid, B Low, C High.

options.label: A · Develop a high-fidelity prototype of the core flows immediately (€22,000, 6 weeks)
options.why: Defendable if the reason is concrete, not in the model: effort Mid by the rule, benefit Mid (it teaches something, but from a polished version of an untested idea), risk Mid (most of the budget goes into an idea nobody has tested).

options.label: B · Test low-fidelity first (€6,500, 2 weeks)
options.why: Reference choice: cheap, fast, and it gives evidence on structure and flow before the money is spent. Benefit High, effort Low, risk Low. The plan's rationale: minimise risk before maximising technology.

options.label: C · Develop directly without testing (€48,000, 11 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: nothing is learned before launch, effort High, benefit Low, risk High; learners find the problems by leaving, and rework would use up the rest of the budget.

optKey.teachingNote: Effort is rule-based (under €10,000 Low, up to €25,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; benefit and risk are judgements and are never marked. The risks without testing are not scored; ticking more is fine.

riskKey.title: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk
riskKey.expected: We buy technology that the data cannot support.

options.label: We buy technology that the data cannot support.
options.why: The central risk of the whole plan: technology against user value. LearnPro's data is incomplete (it knows where learners leave, not why), so technology that the data cannot support is the likeliest failure.

options.label: Competitors' AI gets ahead while we run pilots.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the data risk because the case states incomplete data.

options.label: Learners do not understand or trust the recommendations.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the data risk because the case states incomplete data.

options.label: The pilot is too small to show a result.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the data risk because the case states incomplete data.

options.label: The legal check for adaptive features comes too late.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the data risk because the case states incomplete data.

riskKey.teachingNote: Any of the five defends when the plan to meet it is concrete (what is done, by whom, when). The wrong answer is a risk with no action.

sortKey.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts into Learning path, Short units, Feedback
sortKey.expected: Learning path: fact 1, fact 6  |  Short units: fact 3, fact 5  |  Feedback: fact 2, fact 4, fact 7, fact 8

options.label: Fact 1 · A: a path of six steps, current step marked
options.why: Learning path. It shows the steps in order and which one is next: a learning path.

options.label: Fact 2 · A: progress bar and “Step 2 of 6”
options.why: Feedback. It shows how far along the learner is: feedback on progress.

options.label: Fact 3 · A: each unit “6 min” with one goal
options.why: Short units. It lets the learner finish one unit in a few minutes: short units.

options.label: Fact 4 · A: “4 of 5 correct”, question to review
options.why: Feedback. It gives a result after a task: feedback.

options.label: Fact 5 · B: one long page, about 40 minutes
options.why: Short units. There is no unit a learner can finish in a few minutes: short units are missing.

options.label: Fact 6 · B: no menu, the only way on is to scroll
options.why: Learning path. The steps and their order are not shown: the learning path is missing.

options.label: Fact 7 · B: no sign of how far along
options.why: Feedback. The learner cannot see how far they have come: feedback on progress is missing.

options.label: Fact 8 · B: no message after the last page
options.why: Feedback. No sign of success after the effort: feedback is missing.

sortKey.teachingNote: The sort is objective: each fact answers or fails one of the three questions of card A1 (what next, can I do this in my time, am I getting somewhere). Two edges: fact 2 (progress bar and “Step 2 of 6”) also says where you are on a path, but it shows how far along the learner is, which is feedback; the test question is whether it tells you what to do next (path) or how far you have come (feedback). Fact 6 (no menu) is a missing path, not a missing unit. The preference and the principles are judged: either platform defends if the reason is written from the learner's side. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, compare two platforms, derive three principles.

testKey.title: Block 2.2 · Three UX tests
testKey.expected: Clickable low-fidelity test with 5 learners, think-aloud  |  Drop-out analysis per lesson from existing logs  |  Interviews with 8 learners who left

options.label: T1 · Paper-prototype test with 5 learners, task-based (Qualitative: says why; €3,000, 1 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: a cheap first test of the course start, in one week. It overlaps with the prototype approach if P1 is chosen.

options.label: T2 · Clickable low-fidelity test with 5 learners, think-aloud (Qualitative: says why; €6,000, 2 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it shows whether learners complete a whole flow on the chosen prototype and where they hesitate, in two weeks.

options.label: T3 · Unmoderated remote test with 30 learners (Quantitative: says how many; €9,000, 3 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: a larger count of task success and time, but it does not show why.

options.label: T4 · A/B test of two course-start screens on live traffic (Quantitative: says how many; €12,000, 6 weeks)
options.why: Defendable later, not now: an A/B test needs enough learners and takes six weeks; the platform's size and the 12-week limit make it a poor first choice.

options.label: T5 · Drop-out analysis per lesson from existing logs (Quantitative: says how many; €4,000, 2 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it shows where learners leave, from data that already exists, cheaply. It shows where, not why, so it is paired with an interview test.

options.label: T6 · Interviews with 8 learners who left (Qualitative: says why; €5,000, 2 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: the only test here that can show why learners left, which the case says nobody knows.

options.label: T7 · Usability test of the full high-fidelity redesign (Qualitative and quantitative; €30,000, 8 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: it tests a finished high-fidelity redesign that does not exist yet, at €30,000 and 8 weeks, before the cheap questions are answered.

testKey.teachingNote: A good set mixes kinds: something that shows why (qualitative: T1, T2, T6) with something that shows where or how many (quantitative: T3, T4, T5). Three of the same kind leave half the question open. Cost and weeks are a live hint, not a lock; over the budget or the time still exports with the amount printed.

weakKey.title: Block 2.1 (Optional) · Three main weaknesses
weakKey.expected: Learners get no feedback on what they do or how far they have come.  |  Every learner gets the same path and the same content, whatever they already know.  |  The content is long and passive, with little to do.

options.label: Learners get no feedback on what they do or how far they have come.
options.why: Facts 7 and 8 show it: no sign of progress, no message after the last page.

options.label: Every learner gets the same path and the same content, whatever they already know.
options.why: The case names it: “no personalisation”.

options.label: The content is long and passive, with little to do.
options.why: The case says the content is rated “boring”, and fact 5 shows one long page of about 40 minutes of reading.

options.label: The visual style of the platform looks dated.
options.why: No printed fact says so; it is about the surface, not the experience.

options.label: The course catalogue is too small.
options.why: Nothing in the case says learners leave for lack of courses.

options.label: The subscription price is too high.
options.why: The case mentions no price complaint.

weakKey.teachingNote: The plan's model solution names the main problem as a lack of feedback and individualisation. A learner who swaps one weakness for another and points at a printed fact defends the choice; a weakness with no printed evidence does not.

causeGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · Which printed fact supports your first cause
causeGuide.answer: The case itself names too much information at once, no visual structure and no recognisable learning logic, and facts 1 to 8 show each one; fact 5 shows the unexplained technical terms.
causeGuide.example: At LearnLoop the brief says the lesson shows several boxes next to the text, and one printed fact shows a 700-word page. Those are the causes I can point at; “the logo is old” has nothing printed behind it.
causeGuide.why: A cause is defended by a printed fact. The plan's model solution names the main problem as extraneous cognitive load.
lookFor: Points at a printed fact (by its number) or quotes a case line.
Does not offer a cause the case never mentions.

decisionOrderGuide.title: 3.1 · Why the first measure goes first (Core)
decisionOrderGuide.answer: Rebuilding the ten most-used lessons goes first: it removes extraneous load for the most learners, keeps the content and shows a visible result, so effectiveness and efficiency both rise there.
decisionOrderGuide.example: Rebuilding the most-opened lessons goes first because it meets the most learners and shows a visible result; the content standard follows so that new lessons do not repeat the problem.
decisionOrderGuide.why: The roadmap is an order with a reason. The model order is rebuild, standard, testing routine; a different order defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one.
Says what it does for learning effectiveness and cognitive efficiency.

definitionGuide.title: 3.1 · Your definition of learning-effective UX (Core)
definitionGuide.answer: A learning-effective UX is one in which a beginner can reach the stated learning goal of a lesson with as little unnecessary effort as possible, shown by being able to explain the key point in their own words afterwards.
definitionGuide.example: For LearnLoop: a design is learning-effective when an intermediate learner can reach the unit's goal in the planned time, shown by solving one new task afterwards without help.
definitionGuide.why: Materi B1: the definition names the learner, the goal, the cost to be kept low and the proof. A definition without a proof cannot be tested.
lookFor: Names the learner (intended level).
Names the goal.
Names the cost kept low (effort that does not help learning).
Names the proof (explain or do).
pitfalls: “Easy to use” with no proof of learning.
A satisfaction rating as the only proof.

giveUpGuide.title: 3.2 · What you give up or postpone (Core)
giveUpGuide.answer: I give up the full diagram redesign and the AI summary button this year; learners keep the plain text versions of the less-used lessons for now.
giveUpGuide.example: I give up the new visual brand this year, and I postpone the AI summary tool; learners keep the current look and the plain summaries.
giveUpGuide.why: The skill of Level 3: a decision that gives up nothing has not decided. The answer names something real that a stakeholder would miss.
lookFor: Names a concrete thing given up or postponed.
It is something someone would miss, not a throwaway.

improveGuide.title: 1.1 · What you would improve intuitively (Core)
improveGuide.answer: I would split the lesson into short parts with headings (facts 1 and 4), take the banner, chat and extra menu off the lesson page (fact 2), and state the goal of each lesson and group the 28 lessons in order (facts 7 and 8).
improveGuide.example: At LearnLoop I would put the lesson in three parts with headings, because the page is one block, and I would hide the news banner while someone is reading, because it competes with the text.
improveGuide.why: The plan asks what the learner would improve intuitively. A good answer names a change and the fact it answers, so the change is traceable to the evidence.
lookFor: Names at least two changes, each tied to a fact by its number.
The changes act on the load (amount, form, order), not on the look.

missingGuide.title: 2.2 · What information you are missing (Core)
missingGuide.answer: I do not know whether learners are overloaded by the amount of content or by the wording of the technical terms. I would watch five beginners read Lesson 7 and ask each to explain the key point.
missingGuide.example: I do not know whether learners are overloaded by how much there is or by how it is worded. I would ask six beginners to explain the key point of one lesson before choosing.
missingGuide.why: The plan asks it outright (“Welche Information fehlt Ihnen?”). A good answer names a specific unknown that would change the decision, and a way to find it out.
lookFor: Names a specific unknown, not “more data”.
Says how it could be found out.
Connects to the decision.

optWhyGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · Which option has the greatest effect on learning
optWhyGuide.answer: Splitting the content into small modules has the greatest effect: the learner has less to hold at once and nothing they need is removed. Shortening removes content that beginners came for.
optWhyGuide.example: For a hard beginner course I would say splitting into small modules: the learner holds less at once and nothing is removed. Shortening would take away what the learner came for.
optWhyGuide.why: The plan's rationale: learning capacity before the amount of information. A good answer refers to what the learner has to hold, find or understand.
lookFor: Refers to what the learner holds, finds or understands.
Notes whether needed content is kept.

orderGuide.title: 2.2 · Why the first priority goes first (Core)
orderGuide.answer: Chunking goes first because it removes the biggest load, the 500-word block, for every learner without deleting content. Learning capacity matters more than the amount of information.
orderGuide.example: At LearnLoop the module split goes first: it removes the biggest load for every learner and costs €12,000, and the other measures work better on short units.
orderGuide.why: The plan's rationale: learning capacity > amount of information. A different first priority defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Refers to the learner's problem, the cost or what the others depend on.

reflectGuide.title: 1.3 (Optional) · Coaching reflection
reflectGuide.answer: On the lesson page, where a banner, a chat and a nine-entry menu compete with the text. The key sentence of each lesson and the goal of the lesson: they tell the learner what to hold on to. Splitting lessons into short units, because a learner can then explain what a unit said, which is measurable.
reflectGuide.why: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: UX steers attention and thinking; good UX does not reduce thinking but guides it; “simple” is not the same as “effective for learning”. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.

riskPlanGuide.title: 3.2 · What you do about the biggest risk (Core)
riskPlanGuide.answer: I add a short check at the end of each rebuilt lesson, so that we measure what learners can do next to completion. I would notice the risk if completion rises but the check scores do not.
riskPlanGuide.example: I add a three-question check to every rebuilt lesson, so that we see whether learners can explain the point, not only whether they finish.
riskPlanGuide.why: A risk with no action is only a worry. The action should be concrete: what is done, and when it is noticed. To tell too simple from too complex apart you need a completion measure and a measure of what learners can do.
lookFor: Names an action.
Says when or how the risk would be noticed.

strategyGuide.title: 3.1 · Your strategy to reduce cognitive load (Core)
strategyGuide.answer: I will first reduce what does not help learning, clutter and unstructured text, in the lessons most learners open, and I will protect the professional depth of the content.
strategyGuide.example: At LearnLoop I would first cut the clutter and the wall of text in the most-opened lessons, and protect the worked examples that the learners need to practise.
strategyGuide.why: Materi A2 and B1: cut extraneous load first, keep the intrinsic difficulty the course exists to teach. A strategy that only reduces has not weighed the conflict.
lookFor: Names what is reduced first.
Names what is protected.
One to three sentences.

uncertainGuide.title: 3.2 · The decision without user data (Core)
uncertainGuide.answer: I decide to rebuild one course in small modules and test it with five beginners. I do not know whether learners are overloaded by the amount or by the wording. I will reverse it if fewer than four of five beginners can explain the key point after a lesson.
uncertainGuide.example: I decide to rebuild one course in short units and test it with six beginners. I do not know whether the load comes from length or from wording. I will reverse it if fewer than five of six can explain the key point after a lesson.
uncertainGuide.why: The frame of Materi B3: what I decide, what I do not know, what would make me reverse and by when. A checkable reversal condition has a figure and a time.
lookFor: States the decision.
States what is not known.
Gives a checkable reversal condition with a figure and a time.
pitfalls: A reversal condition no one could check (“if it does not work”).
A decision that waits for data instead of choosing a step that can be undone.

worstGuide.title: 1.1 · The fact that would make a learner stop first, and how the process feels (Core)
worstGuide.answer: I open Lesson 7 and see one block of about 500 words. I would not know where to start, and by the fifth sentence I would have lost track of the first, so I would close the page.
worstGuide.example: At LearnLoop a new learner opens a lesson with a menu, a banner and three boxes next to the text. I would not know what to look at first, and after a minute I would stop reading and scroll to the end.
worstGuide.why: Any of the eight facts defends. What the plan asks for is the user's side (“Beschreiben Sie, wie sich der Lernprozess anfühlt”): the answer must say what the learner cannot do or hold in mind (intake, processing, storage), not that something looks wrong.
lookFor: Written from the learner's side (“I would not know…”, “I would lose track…”).
Names a consequence: a step of learning that fails (what to look at, what to hold, what to keep).
Refers to the fact chosen.

causeKey.title: Block 2.1 (Optional) · Four causes of cognitive overload
causeKey.expected: Too much information is shown at once.  |  The content has no visual structure.  |  The learner cannot see a learning logic: groups, order, goals.  |  Technical terms are used without explanation.

options.label: Too much information is shown at once.
options.why: The case names it, and facts 1 to 3 show it.

options.label: The content has no visual structure.
options.why: The case names it, and facts 4 to 6 show it.

options.label: The learner cannot see a learning logic: groups, order, goals.
options.why: The case names it (“no recognisable learning logic”), and facts 7 and 8 show it.

options.label: Technical terms are used without explanation.
options.why: The case says the text has unexplained technical terms, and fact 5 shows it.

options.label: The subject itself is complex.
options.why: True, and it is the intrinsic load, but it is not a cause of overload that design can remove; design can only order it.

options.label: The visual style of the platform looks dated.
options.why: No printed fact says so; it is about the surface, not the load.

options.label: The course catalogue is too small.
options.why: Nothing in the case says learners are overloaded for lack of courses.

causeKey.teachingNote: The plan's model solution names the main problem as extraneous cognitive load. “The subject itself is complex” is true and is the intrinsic load, but it is not a cause that design can remove; a learner who ticks it and says so defends the choice, and the key marks it as not expected only because the task asks for causes the design can act on.

decisionKey.title: Block 3.1 · Three measures for the strategy
decisionKey.expected: Rebuild the ten most-used lessons; A content standard with editorial review; A learner-testing routine for new content

options.label: D1 · Rebuild the ten most-used lessons (€60,000, 20 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it removes extraneous load for the most learners (Materi B1: structure and chunking first) and keeps the content.

options.label: D2 · A content standard with editorial review (€25,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: a content standard is the decision logic made concrete; every new lesson passes the same checks, so the problem does not return.

options.label: D3 · A learner-testing routine for new content (€30,000, 52 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it is the evidence the case lacks (the plan asks to decide without user data), and it shows both effectiveness and efficiency.

options.label: D4 · Cut the specialist content by a third (€15,000, 8 weeks)
options.why: Rejected in the plan's own logic: the content is professionally necessary, so cutting a third is the over-simplification risk (Materi B2).

options.label: D5 · Result and next step after every lesson (€30,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: feedback after every lesson helps storage and gives a measure of what learners can do; it is a candidate for next year.

options.label: D6 · An AI summary button (€70,000, 24 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: €70,000 and 24 weeks for a tool that shortens lessons on demand, without checking whether the shortened version still teaches.

options.label: D7 · A new visual brand (€45,000, 20 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: it changes the look, not the load; no printed fact is about the look.

decisionKey.teachingNote: A different set of three defends if the reason is written and the three together answer the definition of learning-effective UX. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38); a set over the €150,000 limit exports with the amount printed as a fact.

logicKey.title: Block 3.2 · Who decides, and which checks a new lesson passes
logicKey.expected: Who: The head of learning with the content lead. Checks: One stated learning goal; A size that fits the learner's time; The key sentence is marked; Technical terms are explained in place; A short check or task at the end.

options.label: Who decides: The Chief Learning Experience Officer alone
options.why: Defendable, but one person's taste is exactly what a decision logic should prevent.

options.label: Who decides: The head of learning with the content lead
options.why: Learning judgement and content ownership together: neither one person's taste nor the author's own view.

options.label: Who decides: The author of the lesson
options.why: Rejected: an author checking their own lesson has no outside view.

options.label: Who decides: A steering group with management
options.why: Defendable for large budget items; too slow for every lesson.

options.label: Check: One stated learning goal
options.why: A check that can be done on every lesson and that follows from the three loads.

options.label: Check: A size that fits the learner's time
options.why: A check that can be done on every lesson and that follows from the three loads.

options.label: Check: The key sentence is marked
options.why: A check that can be done on every lesson and that follows from the three loads.

options.label: Check: Technical terms are explained in place
options.why: A check that can be done on every lesson and that follows from the three loads.

options.label: Check: A short check or task at the end
options.why: A check that can be done on every lesson and that follows from the three loads.

options.label: Check: A test with beginners before release
options.why: Defendable and strong, but not on every lesson: five beginners per module before release is the testing routine (D3), not a per-lesson check.

options.label: Check: Approval by the most senior person in the room
options.why: Rejected: authority is not a check on whether a lesson teaches.

logicKey.teachingNote: At least three checks are required; which ones is judged on the reason in the memo, not on matching the model. A style guide that nobody checks is not a decision logic (Materi B3).

measureKey.title: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
measureKey.expected: Chunking; Clear structure; Remove extras from the lesson page; Goal and outline. Total €30,000 of €40,000, longest 3 weeks of 4.

options.label: M1 · Chunking
options.why: Answers a printed fact (amount). Effort Mid by the printed cost €10,000. Reference ratings: impact High, risk Low.

options.label: M2 · Visualisation
options.why: In the plan's own list, and defendable: visualisation helps where a flow or structure is described. At €20,000 and 5 weeks it is High effort and one week over the four-week limit, so the reference set uses “Goal and outline” instead. A learner who funds it exports with the longer time printed as a fact and a reason.

options.label: M3 · Clear structure
options.why: Answers a printed fact (form). Effort Low by the printed cost €7,000. Reference ratings: impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: M4 · Remove extras from the lesson page
options.why: Answers a printed fact (amount). Effort Low by the printed cost €4,000. Reference ratings: impact Mid, risk Mid.

options.label: M5 · Goal and outline
options.why: Answers a printed fact (order). Effort Mid by the printed cost €9,000. Reference ratings: impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: M6 · Points for lesson views
options.why: Rejected: points for lesson views reward opening a lesson, not understanding it, and add one more thing to the screen.

options.label: M7 · New brand look
options.why: Rejected: it changes the look, not the load; no printed fact is about the look.

options.label: M8 · An AI chatbot
options.why: Rejected: €48,000 and 10 weeks is over both limits, and a chatbot adds one more thing to the screen.

options.label: M9 · Extra reading library
options.why: Rejected: more reading material adds load; learners are already overloaded by the amount.

measureKey.teachingNote: Visualisation (M2) takes 5 weeks against the 4-week limit; the reference set uses M5 instead. Effort is rule-based (under €8,000 Low, up to €15,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements and are never marked. A different, well-reasoned choice is acceptable and exports (CLAUDE.md #38): over budget, over time, another set of four, a different order, all with a stated reason. The plan's rationale: learning capacity > amount of information.

optKey.title: Block 1.2 (Optional) · Reduce the load of a module: three options
optKey.expected: Greatest effect: Split the content into small modules. Order: C, B, A. Effort by the printed cost: A Low, B High, C Mid.

options.label: A · Shorten the content significantly (€7,500, 2 weeks)
options.why: Last: the content is professionally necessary and the learners are beginners, so shortening a lot removes what they need. Effort Low, impact Low, risk High.

options.label: B · Visualise the content (diagrams, graphics) (€22,000, 4 weeks)
options.why: Second: a diagram helps where a structure or flow is described, not everywhere; effort High by the rule, and it takes the whole four weeks. Impact Mid, risk Mid.

options.label: C · Split the content into small modules (€10,000, 3 weeks)
options.why: Reference: chunking reduces what the learner holds at once without deleting content. Impact High, effort Mid by the rule, risk Low.

optKey.teachingNote: Effort is rule-based (under €8,000 Low, up to €15,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements and are never marked. The plan's rationale for the day: learning capacity > amount of information.

riskKey.title: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk
riskKey.expected: We measure completion but not what learners can do.

options.label: The content is now so light that learners finish but cannot apply it.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the measurement risk because the plan's question is where the risk of too much simplification lies.

options.label: The content is still too complex, and learners still leave.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the measurement risk because the plan's question is where the risk of too much simplification lies.

options.label: We measure completion but not what learners can do.
options.why: The one that hides both other risks: without a measure of what learners can do, “too simple” and “too complex” cannot be told apart (Materi B2). The remedy is a check at the end of each lesson.

options.label: The budget is used up before a first result is visible.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the measurement risk because the plan's question is where the risk of too much simplification lies.

options.label: Authors ignore the new content standard.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it; the model picks the measurement risk because the plan's question is where the risk of too much simplification lies.

riskKey.teachingNote: Any of the five defends when the plan to meet it is concrete (what is done, by whom, when). The wrong answer is a risk with no action.

sortKey.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts into Amount, Form, Order and purpose
sortKey.expected: Amount: fact 1, fact 2, fact 3  |  Form: fact 4, fact 5, fact 6  |  Order and purpose: fact 7, fact 8

options.label: Fact 1 · One continuous text of about 500 words
options.why: Amount. The learner has to take in 500 words at once: amount.

options.label: Fact 2 · Banner, chat, recommendations and a nine-entry menu next to the text
options.why: Amount. Several things compete for attention at once: amount.

options.label: Fact 3 · All 12 quiz questions on one page
options.why: Amount. Twelve questions at once is a question of how much is shown together: amount.

options.label: Fact 4 · No paragraphs, headings or lists
options.why: Form. The content is not shaped into parts the eye can use: form.

options.label: Fact 5 · No picture, and terms not explained
options.why: Form. The presentation offers neither a picture nor an explanation: form.

options.label: Fact 6 · The key sentence looks like every other sentence
options.why: Form. Nothing marks what matters most, so attention has nothing to follow: form (visual hierarchy).

options.label: Fact 7 · 28 lessons in one flat list
options.why: Order and purpose. The learner cannot see groups or an order: order and purpose.

options.label: Fact 8 · No lesson states its goal or its link to the one before
options.why: Order and purpose. The learner cannot tell what a lesson is for or how it fits: order and purpose.

sortKey.teachingNote: The sort is objective: each fact belongs to one of the three observations of the case. Two edges: fact 5 (no picture, terms not explained) can read as amount of knowledge needed, but what the page offers to explain is a matter of how the content is shaped, so it is Form; fact 3 (12 quiz questions on one page) is Amount even though it is a quiz layout. The one fact that makes a learner stop first and how the process feels are judged: any of the eight defends if the reason is written from the learner's side (intake, processing, storage). Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, describe 5 problems from the user's side.

causeGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · Which printed fact supports your first cause
causeGuide.answer: The case says the content is perceived as boring and that progress is not visible; facts 1 and 8 show a progress bar on one platform and none on the other, and facts 3 and 5 show a task on one and only reading on the other.
causeGuide.example: At LearnLoop the brief says learners start a course and then stop, and one printed fact shows a course page with no end point. Those are the causes I can point at; “the logo is old” has nothing printed behind it.
causeGuide.why: A cause is defended by a printed fact. The plan's model solution names the main problem as the lack of perceived progress and activation.
lookFor: Points at a printed fact (by its number) or quotes a case line.
Does not offer a cause the case never mentions.

decisionOrderGuide.title: 3.1 · Why the first decision goes first (Core)
decisionOrderGuide.answer: Visible progress and a next step go first: they work on ability and prompt for every learner on every page, cost €40,000, and give the first figures (return rate) within fourteen weeks.
decisionOrderGuide.example: A progress display and a next step go first because they work on ability and prompt for every learner, cost less than a rebuild, and show a first figure within three months.
decisionOrderGuide.why: The order is a roadmap with a reason. The model order is visible progress, goals and feedback standard, research routine; a different order defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one.
Says which condition it works on and what it does for retention.

giveUpGuide.title: 3.2 · What you give up or postpone (Core)
giveUpGuide.answer: I give up points, badges and the leaderboard this year, and I postpone rebuilding the five most-used courses; learners keep the current content with a progress display on top.
giveUpGuide.example: I give up the points programme this year and postpone the loss messages; learners keep the plain course pages with a progress display.
giveUpGuide.why: The skill of Level 3: a decision that gives up nothing has not decided. The answer names something real that a stakeholder would miss.
lookFor: Names a concrete thing given up or postponed.
It is something someone would miss, not a throwaway.

missingGuide.title: 2.2 · What information you are missing (Core)
missingGuide.answer: I do not know whether learners leave for lack of progress or for lack of time. I would interview six learners who dropped out and ask what made them stop.
missingGuide.example: I do not know whether learners leave because they see no progress or because they have no time. I would interview six who stopped before choosing.
missingGuide.why: The plan asks it outright. A good answer names a specific unknown that would change the decision, and a way to find it out.
lookFor: Names a specific unknown, not “more data”.
Says how it could be found out.
Connects to the decision.

optWhyGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · Which measure has a lasting effect
optWhyGuide.answer: Visualising progress has a lasting effect: after a reward would stop, the learner still knows how far they have come and what is left, which is information about their own skill and not a payment. Badges and points depend on a continuing reward.
optWhyGuide.example: For LearnLoop I would say a progress and next-step display: after a reward would stop, the learner still sees how far they have come. A weekly leaderboard ends the moment people stop caring about it.
optWhyGuide.why: The plan asks which measure has a lasting effect. A good answer says what remains when a reward would stop.
lookFor: Says what remains after a reward would stop.
Refers to competence, progress or activation rather than to “it is exciting”.

orderGuide.title: 2.2 · Why the first priority goes first (Core)
orderGuide.answer: Progress tracking goes first: it is the cheapest of the four that works for every learner, it answers the strongest motivator, and the other measures show up in it as steps done.
orderGuide.example: At LearnLoop the progress display goes first: it helps every learner, costs €8,000, and the other measures show up in it as steps done.
orderGuide.why: The plan's rationale: perceived progress is the strongest motivator. A different first priority defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Refers to the learner's problem, the cost or what the others depend on.

preferGuide.title: 1.1 · Which platform is more motivating, and why (Core)
preferGuide.answer: On Platform A I can see that I am 40% through, I do a short task instead of only reading, I am told what I can do after the unit, and I get a result and a next step. On Platform B I would not know how far I am or what any of it is for, so I would stop.
preferGuide.example: At LearnLoop I would prefer the version where I see “3 of 8 done” and finish each unit with a short task and a message. I can tell how far I have come and what to do next; on the other version I only scroll.
