preferGuide.why: The plan asks which platform is more motivating and why. A good answer is written from the learner's side (“I can see…”, “I do…”) and names something the learner can see, do or feel on one platform and not on the other.
lookFor: Written from the learner's side.
Names at least one thing that is on one platform and missing on the other.
Not “it looks better”.

principlesGuide.title: 1.1 · Three principles of motivation (Core)
principlesGuide.answer: Show the learner their progress, because people continue when they can see they are getting somewhere. | Let the learner do something in every unit, because doing keeps attention and builds the skill the unit is about. | State what the learner will be able to do and give a result after each task, because a goal and a result tell them what the effort is for.
principlesGuide.example: Show how far the learner has come, because people speed up when they can see the end. | Give a result after every task, because a learner who gets no answer cannot tell whether the effort counted. | Start a unit with what the learner will be able to do, because a goal makes a task worth doing.
principlesGuide.why: Materi A2: a principle of motivation is a sentence with a reason, “Do X, because Y”. Three principles from the differences between the platforms: progress, activation, goals or feedback.
lookFor: Each is one sentence “Do X, because Y”.
Each reason says what the learner experiences.
They are drawn from the differences, not from general advice.
pitfalls: A slogan with no reason (“Make it fun”).
A principle about rewards where the facts are about progress and activation.

reflectGuide.title: 1.3 (Optional) · Coaching reflection
reflectGuide.answer: Progress that is real and feedback after each task: they change what the learner does next, not only how the screen looks. Motivation that stays when the reward stops: a goal I care about, a sign that I am getting better, a choice in how I learn. Loss messages and rankings of the weakest learners: they raise activity today and cost trust tomorrow.
reflectGuide.why: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: motivation is not gamification; engagement arises from structure, not only from rewards; UX can also demotivate. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.

riskPlanGuide.title: 3.2 · What you do about the biggest risk (Core)
riskPlanGuide.answer: I run the research and experiment routine from month one, so we learn why learners leave before we spend the large part of the budget. I would notice the risk if the interviews name a reason the measures do not touch.
riskPlanGuide.example: I give each reward a check on the cheapest way to earn it, and I look at whether learners finish units, not only open them. I would notice the risk if opened lessons rise while finished ones do not.
riskPlanGuide.why: A risk with no action is only a worry. The action is concrete: what is done, and when it is noticed.
lookFor: Names an action.
Says when or how the risk would be noticed.

strategyWhyGuide.title: 3.1 · Why this motivation strategy (Core)
strategyWhyGuide.answer: I build on intrinsic motivation (goals, progress, feedback) and keep extrinsic elements out, because the leaving learners lack a sign of progress and a next step, which are ability and prompt problems; a reward would not fix those.
strategyWhyGuide.example: For LearnLoop I would lean on a mix with intrinsic as the base: learners who stop do not see a next step, which is an ability problem, so I would fix that first and add a small, honest reward later.
strategyWhyGuide.why: Materi B1: behaviour needs motivation, ability and a prompt together. A strategy that works only on motivation is incomplete, and a reward where the barrier is ability is the place where motivation is overestimated.
lookFor: Names which condition (motivation, ability, prompt) the strategy works on.
Names for which learners.
Does not claim that a reward fixes an ability problem.

successGuide.title: 3.1 · Your success sentence (Core)
successGuide.answer: I will measure the seven-day return rate against today's baseline, with a control group that does not get the progress display, and I will read it after six weeks together with six learner interviews.
successGuide.example: At LearnLoop I would compare the share of new learners who return within seven days against last quarter's figure, with half of them seeing the old page, and read it after eight weeks together with five interviews.
successGuide.why: Materi B3: success has a baseline, a target, a method and a date, written before the change. A behaviour metric and a reason-giving method together.
lookFor: Names the metric and a baseline.
Names a method (control group, interviews).
Names a time.
pitfalls: “We will see whether it improves.”
Time spent or badges earned as the only evidence.

uncertainGuide.title: 3.2 · The decision under uncertainty (Core)
uncertainGuide.answer: I decide to add a progress display and a next step to the three most-opened courses first. I do not know whether learners leave for lack of progress or lack of time. I will reverse it if the seven-day return rate is not at least five points above the control group after six weeks.
uncertainGuide.example: I decide to show a next-step button in two courses first. I do not know whether learners leave for lack of direction or lack of time. I will reverse it if the seven-day return rate is not four points above the control group after eight weeks.
uncertainGuide.why: The frame of Materi B3: what I decide, what I do not know, what would make me reverse and by when. A checkable reversal condition has a figure and a time.
lookFor: States the decision.
States what is not known.
Gives a checkable reversal condition with a figure and a time.
pitfalls: A reversal condition no one could check (“if it does not work”).
A decision that waits for data instead of choosing a step that can be undone.

causeKey.title: Block 2.1 (Optional) · Three main causes of the motivation problem
causeKey.expected: Learners cannot see their progress.  |  The content is passive: reading without doing.  |  Goals and results are unclear: no stated goal, no feedback.

options.label: Learners cannot see their progress.
options.why: The case names it (“no visible progress”), and facts 1 and 8 show the difference between the platforms.

options.label: The content is passive: reading without doing.
options.why: The case says the content is perceived as “boring”, and facts 3 and 5 show that one platform has tasks and the other only reading.

options.label: Goals and results are unclear: no stated goal, no feedback.
options.why: Platform B has long content, no feedback and unclear goals (the plan), and facts 2, 4, 6 and 7 show it.

options.label: The platform gives too few rewards, such as badges.
options.why: No printed fact says so. Platform A motivates without any reward (Materi A1: motivation is not the same as gamification).

options.label: The subscription price is too high.
options.why: Nothing in the case mentions the price.

options.label: The course catalogue is too small.
options.why: Learners start courses; the problem is that they drop out, not that there is too little to start.

causeKey.teachingNote: The plan's main problem is the lack of perceived progress and of activation. “Too few rewards” is the popular wrong answer: Platform A motivates without any reward, so the missing reward is not what the facts show. A learner who ticks it and points at a printed fact defends the choice.

decisionKey.title: Block 3.1 · Three prioritised measures
decisionKey.expected: Visible progress and a next step across the platform; A goals and feedback standard; A research and experiment routine

options.label: D1 · Visible progress and a next step across the platform (€40,000, 14 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it works on ability and prompt for every learner on every page (Materi B1) and is the strongest motivator in the plan's logic.

options.label: D2 · Rebuild the five most-used courses with short interactive tasks (€70,000, 24 weeks)
options.why: Defendable and strong on activation, but €70,000 and 24 weeks: the biggest share of the budget before any evidence.

options.label: D3 · A goals and feedback standard (€25,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: a goals and feedback standard keeps every new unit and task on the principles, so the problem does not return.

options.label: D4 · Points, badges and a leaderboard (€45,000, 16 weeks)
options.why: Rejected in the plan's own logic: an extrinsic layer on a platform whose problem is missing progress and activation (perverse-incentive risk).

options.label: D5 · A research and experiment routine (€30,000, 52 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: the data is incomplete (the plan), so the research and experiment routine is the evidence the case lacks (Materi B3).

options.label: D6 · Streaks, reminders and loss messages (€20,000, 8 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: loss messages are pressure; they risk trust (Materi B2).

options.label: D7 · Discounts for completion (€35,000, 10 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: a discount after completion only reaches learners who already finish.

decisionKey.teachingNote: A different set of three defends if the reason is written and the three together deal with the three conditions of behaviour. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38); a set over the €180,000 limit exports with the amount printed as a fact.

logicKey.title: Block 3.2 · Who decides, and on what evidence
logicKey.expected: Who: The head of product together with the learning lead. Evidence: An A/B test with a control group; Learner interviews; Return rate and completion data.

options.label: Who decides: The Chief Experience Officer alone
options.why: Defendable, but one person's taste is exactly what a decision architecture should prevent.

options.label: Who decides: The head of product together with the learning lead
options.why: Product and learning judgement together: neither one person's taste nor whoever shouts loudest.

options.label: Who decides: A steering group with management
options.why: Defendable for large budget items; too slow for every optimisation.

options.label: Who decides: Whoever runs the campaign
options.why: Rejected: the campaign owner judges their own work.

options.label: Evidence: An A/B test with a control group
options.why: Evidence about learners' behaviour and reasons (Materi B3).

options.label: Evidence: Learner interviews
options.why: Evidence about learners' behaviour and reasons (Materi B3).

options.label: Evidence: Return rate and completion data
options.why: Evidence about learners' behaviour and reasons (Materi B3).

options.label: Evidence: A comparison with a competitor
options.why: Defendable as context, but a competitor's feature is not proof that it causes their retention (Materi B1).

options.label: Evidence: The opinion of the most senior person in the room
options.why: Rejected: a senior opinion alone is not evidence (Materi B3).

logicKey.teachingNote: At least two kinds of evidence are required; which ones is judged on the reason in the memo, not on matching the model.

measureKey.title: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
measureKey.expected: Progress tracking; Interactive elements; Clear learning objectives; Feedback after every task. Total €44,000 of €40,000, longest 6 weeks of 8.

options.label: M1 · Progress tracking
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (progress). Effort Low by the printed cost €8,000. Reference ratings: impact High, risk Low.

options.label: M2 · Interactive elements
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (activation). Effort Mid by the printed cost €18,000. Reference ratings: impact High, risk Mid.

options.label: M3 · Clear learning objectives
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (goals). Effort Low by the printed cost €6,000. Reference ratings: impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: M4 · Feedback after every task
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (feedback). Effort Mid by the printed cost €12,000. Reference ratings: impact High, risk Low.

options.label: M5 · Points and badges
options.why: Rejected: points and badges reward opening a lesson, not learning (a perverse incentive, Materi B2), and the facts show missing progress and activation, not a missing reward.

options.label: M6 · A public leaderboard
options.why: Rejected: a public ranking rewards the already active and can push the weakest learners out, who are the ones the platform is losing (pressure and comparison, Materi B2).

options.label: M7 · Streaks with loss messages
options.why: Rejected: loss messages are pressure and a manipulation risk; they raise activity today and cost trust tomorrow.

options.label: M8 · Discount coupons for finishing
options.why: Rejected: €22,000 for a discount after completion, which only reaches learners who already finish.

options.label: M9 · New course images and look
options.why: Rejected: it changes the look, not the motivation; no printed fact is about the look.

measureKey.teachingNote: The plan's four measures cost €44,000 against the case's €40,000 (a Case assumption): the reference set is €4,000 over and says where the money goes. Effort is rule-based (under €10,000 Low, up to €20,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements and are never marked. A different, well-reasoned choice is acceptable and exports (CLAUDE.md #38): within the budget, over it, another set of four, a different order, all with a stated reason. The plan's rationale: perceived progress is the strongest motivator.

metricKey.title: Block 3.1 · How to measure success
metricKey.expected: Completion rate; Return rate within seven days; Tasks done per week; Learner interviews

options.label: Completion rate
options.why: A behaviour metric: it counts what learners do and has a baseline (Materi A4, B3).

options.label: Return rate within seven days
options.why: A behaviour metric: it counts what learners do and has a baseline (Materi A4, B3).

options.label: Tasks done per week
options.why: A behaviour metric: it counts what learners do and has a baseline (Materi A4, B3).

options.label: Time spent on the platform
options.why: Ambiguous: a long time can mean interest or confusion; do not use it alone (Materi A4).

options.label: Badges earned
options.why: Rejected: badges earned measure the reward system, not learning.

options.label: Learner interviews
options.why: A method about reasons, to pair with the behaviour metrics (Materi A4).

options.label: Satisfaction rating
options.why: Defendable as an addition, but a rating is an opinion and not behaviour; pair it with a behaviour metric.

metricKey.teachingNote: At least three are required; which ones is judged on the success sentence: a baseline, a target, a method and a date. A metric without a baseline cannot show improvement.

optKey.title: Block 1.2 (Optional) · Choose an engagement strategy: three options
optKey.expected: Lasting effect: Visualise learning progress. Order: B, C, A. Effort by the printed cost: A Mid, B Low, C High.

options.label: A · Gamification: badges and points (€18,000, 5 weeks)
options.why: Last: badges and points are extrinsic rewards. Effort Mid, impact Low for the learners who are leaving, risk High (overjustification: the reward can become the reason, Materi A1). A different order defends if the reason says what remains when the reward stops.

options.label: B · Visualise learning progress (€7,000, 3 weeks)
options.why: Reference: progress is information about the learner's own skill, so it remains when a reward would stop. Effort Low by the rule, impact High, risk Low. The plan's rationale: perceived progress is the strongest motivator.

options.label: C · Make content more interactive (€24,000, 7 weeks)
options.why: Second: making content interactive builds activation and competence and also lasts, but at €24,000 and 7 of the 8 weeks it is High effort and Mid risk (weak tasks feel like homework). Impact High.

optKey.teachingNote: Effort is rule-based (under €10,000 Low, up to €20,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; impact and risk are judgements and are never marked. “Which measure has a lasting effect” has one reference answer (B) but C also defends when the learner says what the learner can do afterwards.

riskKey.title: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk
riskKey.expected: We change the wrong thing because our data does not show why learners leave.

options.label: Learners collect rewards without learning (a perverse incentive).
options.why: The classic perverse incentive (Materi B2): defendable as the biggest risk if the plan has any reward in it; the model plan has none.

options.label: Learners feel pressured and trust the platform less.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it.

options.label: We raise short-term activity that fades once the novelty is gone.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it.

options.label: We change the wrong thing because our data does not show why learners leave.
options.why: The risk the case itself names: the data is incomplete, so the team may fix the wrong thing. The remedy is the research routine before the big spend.

options.label: Management expects retention to rise within weeks.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it.

riskKey.teachingNote: Any of the five defends when the plan to meet it is concrete (what is done, by whom, when). The wrong answer is a risk with no action.

sortKey.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts into four principles
sortKey.expected: Visible progress: fact 1, fact 8  |  Activation: fact 3, fact 5  |  Clear goals: fact 4, fact 7  |  Feedback: fact 2, fact 6

options.label: Fact 1 · A: progress bar “40% done”
options.why: Visible progress. The learner can see how far they have come: visible progress.

options.label: Fact 2 · A: “Correct.” and “Next: task 4”
options.why: Feedback. A result and a next step after an action: feedback.

options.label: Fact 3 · A: a three-minute task the learner does
options.why: Activation. The learner does something related to the goal: activation.

options.label: Fact 4 · A: “After this unit you can…”
options.why: Clear goals. The unit says what the learner will be able to do: a clear goal.

options.label: Fact 5 · B: one long page of reading, no task
options.why: Activation. The learner only reads and never does anything: activation is missing.

options.label: Fact 6 · B: no tick, no message after the last page
options.why: Feedback. Nothing answers the learner's action with a result or a next step: feedback is missing.

options.label: Fact 7 · B: no statement of what you will be able to do
options.why: Clear goals. The learner cannot tell what the course is for: a clear goal is missing.

options.label: Fact 8 · B: no progress, no end point
options.why: Visible progress. The learner cannot see how far they have come or how far it is to the end: visible progress is missing.

sortKey.teachingNote: The sort is objective: each fact belongs to one principle, and each principle has one fact on Platform A and one on Platform B. Two edges: fact 2 (“Correct.” and “Next: task 4”) is Feedback, not Activation, although it follows a task; fact 6 (nothing after the last page) is the missing Feedback, not missing Progress. Which platform is more motivating is judged, but Platform A has all four principles on screen and Platform B none, so any defence of B has to name something the facts do not show. The three principles are “Do X, because Y” sentences: look for a reason, not a slogan. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, describe 5 differences and derive 3 principles.

strategyKey.title: Block 3.1 · Motivation strategy
strategyKey.expected: A mix: intrinsic as the base, a few extrinsic elements

options.label: Mainly intrinsic: goals, competence, progress
options.why: Defendable: it is the cleanest against overjustification, but it ignores that many Habmann learners are required to learn and already have an extrinsic reason.

options.label: A mix: intrinsic as the base, a few extrinsic elements
options.why: Reference: intrinsic as the base, because lasting motivation needs goals, competence and progress (Materi A1), with at most a few extrinsic elements that give real information.

options.label: Mainly extrinsic: points, badges, rewards
options.why: Rejected unless defended: rewards alone raise short-term activity and carry the overjustification and perverse-incentive risks (Materi A1, B2).

strategyKey.teachingNote: The plan's question is intrinsic against extrinsic. The answer is judged on the field under it: which of the three conditions (motivation, ability, prompt) the strategy works on, and for which learners.

conflictGuide.title: 3.1 · The conflict analysis (Core)
conflictGuide.answer: D1: A home screen with one main action and a continue entry. / More completion and fewer support requests. / Fewer places for promotions on the home screen. | D4: Changes that rest on what learners say and do. / Fewer wrong bets and a figure for every decision. / Money and time that could have gone into visible features this year. | D5: Fewer features nobody asked for. / A roadmap that managers can defend with a metric. / Sales loses the right to add a feature without a named user problem.
conflictGuide.example: At LearnLoop, a simpler menu: the user gets the course in one click; the business gets fewer support requests; what is lost is a promotion slot on the home screen, which moves to the course page.
conflictGuide.why: Materi B2: name what the user, the business and the other side get or lose. A decision that serves only one goal is a trade-off: say what the others lose and how you limit the loss.
lookFor: Three short entries per decision.
What is lost or postponed is something someone would miss.
Counts the business gain in completion or support, not in banners.

decisionOrderGuide.title: 3.1 · Why the first decision goes first (Core)
decisionOrderGuide.answer: Rebuilding the navigation and home screen goes first: it fixes what every learner meets, costs €60,000, and gives the first figures (completion) within eighteen weeks, while the research programme and the approval rule start at once beside it.
decisionOrderGuide.example: A task-based home screen goes first because it helps every learner and the business sees completion rise within a few months; the approval rule follows so that new features do not undo it.
decisionOrderGuide.why: The roadmap is an order with a reason. The model order is rebuild, research programme, approval rule; a different order defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one.
Says what it does for the user and for the business.

errorGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · The design error behind each problem
errorGuide.answer: Facts 4 and 5: 14 filters and three lists mean no single clear place to look. | Facts 1 and 2: labels name the software, not the learner's task. | Facts 3 and 4: 22 entries, 9 widgets, 4 banners and 14 filters at once. | Facts 6 and 8: no “Continue where you stopped”, and title and path both read “Home”.
errorGuide.example: At LearnLoop: “Learners cannot find their course” rests on one printed fact, a home screen with nine menu entries and no continue entry. The design error is that the menu follows the company's departments, not the learner's task.
errorGuide.why: A user problem is something a learner cannot do or feel, and you can point at it. The design error names what in the design causes it and the fact number that shows it.
lookFor: Names a design error (system logic, many choices, missing orientation).
Points at a fact number.

expectationsGuide.title: 1.1 · Three expectations of a good platform (Core)
expectationsGuide.answer: I expect to see my course first when I open the platform, because I come with one goal. I expect labels in words I use, because I do not know what a module instance is. I expect to see how far I have come, because I study next to my job and need to know what is left.
expectationsGuide.example: I expect my current course to be the first thing I see, because I arrive with one goal. I expect buttons in words I use, because I do not want to learn the platform's vocabulary. I expect to know where I am, because I jump between devices.
expectationsGuide.why: The plan asks for three expectations. Each starts “I expect…” and ties to a goal or a situation (Materi A2): the expectation behind a frustration.
lookFor: Three, each starting “I expect…”.
Each tied to a goal or situation, with a “because”.
Not a feature list.

giveUpGuide.title: 3.2 · What you give up or postpone (Core)
giveUpGuide.answer: I give up the social feed, groups and badges that sales asked for this year, and I postpone the growth marketing push; sales gets a date to come back with a named user problem.
giveUpGuide.example: I give up the new chat feature this year and postpone the extra courses; sales gets a date to return with a named learner problem.
giveUpGuide.why: The skill of Level 3: a decision that gives up nothing has not decided. The answer names something real that a stakeholder would miss.
lookFor: Names a concrete thing given up or postponed.
It is something someone would miss, not a throwaway.

goalGuide.title: 1.1 · Your goal as a learner (Core)
goalGuide.answer: I want to carry on with the course I started, on my phone, between two meetings, with about ten minutes. It is voluntary, but my manager expects me to finish it this quarter.
goalGuide.example: At LearnLoop I want to finish the data-protection course before Friday, on my laptop at my desk, in the half hour after lunch. It is mandatory, so I just want to get it done.
goalGuide.why: The plan asks what the learner's goals are. A good answer is a task in everyday words (“carry on where I stopped”) and names the situation: device, time, mandatory or voluntary (Materi A2).
lookFor: A task, not a feature wish.
Names a situation: device, time, mandatory or voluntary.
Written from the learner's side.

missingGuide.title: 2.2 · What information you are missing (Core)
missingGuide.answer: I do not know whether learners fail to find content because of the menu or because of the search. I would run a usability test with five learners on the home screen before the rebuild.
missingGuide.example: I do not know whether learners leave because they cannot find the course or because the course is too long. I would watch five learners try to find their course on a Monday morning.
missingGuide.why: The plan asks it outright. A good answer names a specific unknown that would change the decision, and a way to find it out.
lookFor: Names a specific unknown, not “more data”.
Says how it could be found out.
Connects to the decision.

needsGuide.title: 3.1 · The central user needs (Core)
needsGuide.answer: A learner on the move wants to carry on where they stopped, so the business gets completion. A learner who is new wants to find the right course at once, so the business gets usage of paid content. A training manager wants to see that staff finish, so the business gets renewals.
needsGuide.example: At LearnLoop: a team lead wants to assign a course in two clicks, so the business gets more courses finished. A new hire wants to see what to do on day one, so the business gets faster onboarding.
needsGuide.why: Materi B1: state each need as a sentence with three parts: who, what they want to do, and what the business gets if they can. A need without a business link will not get funded.
lookFor: Two or three needs.
Each names who and a task.
Each names a business figure that depends on it.

optWhyGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · Justify your decision
optWhyGuide.answer: Simplifying the navigation goes first: learners find their course and see what to do next, and the business gets more completion and fewer complaints, which are the figures management watches. More content and new features depend on learners finding them first.
optWhyGuide.example: For LearnLoop I would simplify the menu first: learners find their course, so completion rises and support requests fall, which management watches. New features would not be found by the learners who are lost.
optWhyGuide.why: The plan asks to justify the decision. A good answer says what the business gets from the first priority, so that it could be argued to management (Materi A5, B1).
lookFor: Says what the business gets (completion, retention, complaints).
Says what the user gets.
Names why the others come later.

orderGuide.title: 2.2 · Why the first priority goes first (Core)
orderGuide.answer: Clear navigation goes first: it fixes what every learner meets on the first screen, answers three facts, and the other three measures work on top of a menu that makes sense. Understanding users matters more than the number of features.
orderGuide.example: At LearnLoop the task-based menu goes first: it fixes what every learner meets on the first screen, and the other measures work better on top of a menu that makes sense.
orderGuide.why: The plan's rationale: understanding users beats the number of features. A different first priority defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Refers to the learner's problem, the cost or what the others depend on.

reflectGuide.title: 1.3 (Optional) · Coaching reflection
reflectGuide.answer: Adding the social feed because sales asked: nobody asked a learner, and 2% open it. When growth is counted in sign-ups, not in finished courses: the platform then favours banners and promotions over a clear path. By using their numbers: completion, support requests and renewals depend on learners finding and finishing a course, so the user-centred measure is the business measure.
reflectGuide.why: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: user-centredness is not a nice-to-have; organisations often do not act in a user-centred way; UX is a translation effort between user and business. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.

riskPlanGuide.title: 3.2 · What you do about the biggest risk (Core)
riskPlanGuide.answer: I start the research programme in month one, so the first usability test and the interviews with leavers run before the rebuild is signed off. I would notice the risk if the interviews name a problem the plan does not address.
riskPlanGuide.example: I run three learner interviews and a usability test before we sign off the new menu, so that we fix what learners meet, not what we assume. I would notice the risk if the interviews name a problem we did not plan for.
riskPlanGuide.why: A risk with no action is only a worry. The action is concrete: what is done, and when it is noticed.
lookFor: Names an action.
Says when or how the risk would be noticed.

ruleGuide.title: 3.2 · The rule every new feature must pass (Core)
ruleGuide.answer: Every new feature needs a named user problem, a metric and an owner before it enters the roadmap.
ruleGuide.example: Before a feature enters the roadmap, the requester names the learner problem it solves, the figure that will show it worked, and who owns it; otherwise it waits.
ruleGuide.why: Materi B3: a feature approval rule is the most direct decision architecture against feature creep: a named user problem, a metric and an owner.
lookFor: Names a user problem.
Names a metric.
Names an owner.
One or two sentences.

uncertainGuide.title: 3.2 · The decision without complete user data (Core)
uncertainGuide.answer: I decide to rebuild the home screen around one main action and to pause new features for six months. I do not know whether learners leave because of the menu or the search. I will reverse it if completion has not risen by three points after four months.
uncertainGuide.example: I decide to put a “Continue” button on the home screen of two courses first. I do not know whether learners leave because of the menu or the search. I will reverse it if completion in those courses has not risen by two points after three months.
uncertainGuide.why: The frame of Materi B3: what I decide, what I do not know, what would make me reverse and by when. A checkable reversal condition has a figure and a time.
lookFor: States the decision.
States what is not known.
Gives a checkable reversal condition with a figure and a time.
pitfalls: A reversal condition no one could check (“if it does not work”).
A decision that waits for data instead of choosing a step that can be undone.

worstGuide.title: 1.1 · Why this fact frustrates you most (Core)
worstGuide.answer: I come back after three days and expect to see my course and a button that says carry on. Instead the home screen shows menus and banners, and I have to open the course list again and find my place myself.
worstGuide.example: At LearnLoop I open the app expecting my course on top and see five banners. I have to scroll to find it, and by then I have forgotten what I came for.
worstGuide.why: Any of the eight facts defends. What the plan asks for is the user's perspective: say what you expected to see and what you saw instead, as a learner, not as a design opinion.
lookFor: “I expected… I saw…”.
Written as a feeling and a consequence, not “it looks bad”.
Refers to the fact chosen.

causeKey.title: Block 2.1 (Optional) · Four central user problems and their causes
causeKey.expected: Learners cannot find the content they need.  |  Learners do not understand what the buttons and menu entries mean.  |  Learners are overwhelmed by the number of options at once.  |  Learners do not know what to do next.

options.label: Learners cannot find the content they need.
options.why: The case names it, and facts 4, 5 and 6 show why.

options.label: Learners do not understand what the buttons and menu entries mean.
options.why: Facts 1 and 2 show labels in the software's words.

options.label: Learners are overwhelmed by the number of options at once.
options.why: Fact 3 and fact 4 show many choices before any action.

options.label: Learners do not know what to do next.
options.why: Facts 6 and 8 show no “continue” and no sign of where they are.

options.label: Learners want more social features.
options.why: Fact 7 says the opposite: a social feature exists and 2% open it.

options.label: Learners find the price too high.
options.why: Nothing in the case mentions the price.

options.label: The visual style looks dated.
options.why: No printed fact is about the look; it is about the surface, not the learner's task.

causeKey.teachingNote: The plan's main problem is the lack of user-centredness: system logic instead of user logic. “More social features” is the popular wrong answer and fact 7 contradicts it. A learner who ticks it and points at a printed fact defends the choice; the design error written beside each chosen problem is judged on whether it names a fact number.

decisionKey.title: Block 3.1 · Three strategic UX decisions
decisionKey.expected: Rebuild navigation and home screen around learner tasks; A user-research programme; A feature approval rule

options.label: D1 · Rebuild navigation and home screen around learner tasks (€60,000, 18 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it fixes what every learner meets and carries the plan's rationale, understanding users over the number of features (Materi B1).

options.label: D2 · A feature audit (€30,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: a feature audit calms the platform cheaply; strong if the learner pairs it with the approval rule.

options.label: D3 · One content structure (€45,000, 16 weeks)
options.why: Defendable and strong on orientation, but €45,000 and 16 weeks; D1 already carries a continue entry.

options.label: D4 · A user-research programme (€35,000, 52 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: the user data is incomplete (the plan), so the research programme is the evidence the case lacks and feeds every later decision (Materi B3).

options.label: D5 · A feature approval rule (€15,000, 8 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: a feature approval rule is the concrete decision architecture against feature creep (Materi B3).

options.label: D6 · The feature set sales asked for (€90,000, 28 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: €90,000 for the features sales asked for, with no named user problem (Materi B2).

options.label: D7 · A growth marketing push (€60,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: it counts growth in sign-ups on a platform where learners cannot find or finish a course (Materi B1).

decisionKey.teachingNote: A different set of three defends if the reason is written and the conflict analysis names what the user, the business and the other side get or lose. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38); a set over the €200,000 limit exports with the amount printed as a fact.

logicKey.title: Block 3.2 · Who decides, and on what evidence
logicKey.expected: Who: The head of product with the UX lead. Evidence: A usability test; Interviews with learners who left; Usage data per feature.

options.label: Who decides: The Chief UX Strategist alone
options.why: Defendable, but one person's taste is what a decision architecture should prevent.

options.label: Who decides: The head of product with the UX lead
options.why: Product and UX judgement together: the person who owns the roadmap and the person who knows the users.

options.label: Who decides: A steering group with all stakeholders
options.why: Defendable for large budget items; too slow, and all stakeholders pull in different directions (the plan).

options.label: Who decides: Whichever department pays
options.why: Rejected: whoever pays decides by budget, not by user problem.

options.label: Evidence: A usability test
options.why: Evidence about what learners do and why (Materi A4, B3).

options.label: Evidence: Interviews with learners who left
options.why: Evidence about what learners do and why (Materi A4, B3).

options.label: Evidence: Usage data per feature
options.why: Evidence about what learners do and why (Materi A4, B3).

options.label: Evidence: A request from sales
options.why: Defendable as input, but a request from sales says what one department wants, not what users need (Materi B3).

options.label: Evidence: The opinion of the most senior person in the room
options.why: Rejected: a senior opinion alone is not evidence.

logicKey.teachingNote: At least two kinds of evidence are required; which ones is judged on the rule in the memo, not on matching the model. A feature approval rule needs a named user problem, a metric and an owner (Materi B3).

measureKey.title: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, order them
measureKey.expected: Clear navigation; Reduce complexity; Focus on core tasks; Better structuring of content. Total €45,000 of €40,000, longest 5 weeks of 13.

options.label: M1 · Clear navigation
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (orientation). Effort Mid by the printed cost €14,000. Reference ratings: user value High, risk Mid.

options.label: M2 · Reduce complexity
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (complexity). Effort Low by the printed cost €6,000. Reference ratings: user value Mid, risk Low.

options.label: M3 · Focus on core tasks
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (focus). Effort Low by the printed cost €9,000. Reference ratings: user value High, risk Low.

options.label: M4 · Better structuring of content
options.why: The plan's own measure; answers a printed fact (orientation). Effort Mid by the printed cost €16,000. Reference ratings: user value High, risk Mid.

options.label: M5 · Learner language
options.why: Defendable and cheap (€5,000): it answers facts 1 and 2 directly. A learner who takes it in place of better structuring stays inside the budget and leaves fact 5 open; the reason should say so.

options.label: M6 · Six new features
options.why: Rejected: €45,000 and 12 weeks for features sales asked for, on a platform whose problem is too many features nobody uses (fact 7).

options.label: M7 · Twenty new courses
options.why: Rejected: a longer catalogue is harder to search, and learners already cannot find content.

options.label: M8 · A campaign for existing features
options.why: Rejected: advertising features that 2% use does not fix finding or understanding.

options.label: M9 · User research
options.why: Defendable: it closes an evidence gap cheaply, but nothing changes on screen yet; as a fourth measure it leaves the printed problems unanswered.

measureKey.teachingNote: The plan's four measures cost €45,000 against the case's €40,000 (a Case assumption): the reference set is €5,000 over and says where the money goes. Effort is rule-based (under €10,000 Low, up to €20,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; user value and risk are judgements and are never marked. A different, well-reasoned choice is acceptable and exports (CLAUDE.md #38): within the budget, over it, another set of four, a different order, all with a stated reason. The plan's rationale: understanding users beats the number of features.

optKey.title: Block 1.2 (Optional) · User-centredness against business goals
optKey.expected: First priority: Simplify the navigation (a UX goal). Order: B, A, C.

options.label: A · Add more content (a business goal) (€30,000, 8 weeks)
options.why: Second: more content serves a business goal, but learners who cannot find what exists will not find more; user value Low, business value Mid, risk Mid. It defends only if the learner says what the business gets and how learners will find it.

options.label: B · Simplify the navigation (a UX goal) (€11,000, 4 weeks)
options.why: Reference: simplifying the navigation gives users what they miss (user value High) and the business completion and fewer complaints (business value High). Effort Mid by the printed cost, risk Low: structure changes, content stays.

options.label: C · Develop new features (a marketing goal) (€28,000, 10 weeks)
options.why: Last: new features serve a marketing goal on a platform whose problem is the opposite of too few features; user value Low, risk High (a large share of the budget on an unrequested extra).

optKey.teachingNote: All three ratings are judgements here and are never marked; the plan's rationale for the day is that understanding users beats the number of features. A different order defends if the justification names what the business gets from the first priority.

riskKey.title: Block 3.2 · The biggest risk
riskKey.expected: We fixed the wrong user problem because our data was incomplete.

options.label: We fixed the wrong user problem because our data was incomplete.
options.why: The risk the case itself names: the user data is incomplete, so the team may fix the wrong problem. The remedy is the research programme before the big spend.

options.label: Sales and management overrode the plan with their own features.
options.why: Defendable: the stakeholders pursue different goals (the plan); the approval rule is the remedy.

options.label: We measured sign-ups, not finished courses, and growth did not come.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it.

options.label: The changes confused learners who had learned the old platform.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it.

options.label: We spent the budget before a first result was visible.
options.why: Defendable as the biggest risk if the learner says what they do about it.

riskKey.teachingNote: The plan names wrong prioritisation as the greatest risk. Any of the five defends when the plan to meet it is concrete (what is done, by whom, when). The wrong answer is a risk with no action.

sortKey.title: Block 1.1 · Eight facts into three mistakes
sortKey.expected: Functions instead of benefits: fact 1, fact 2, fact 7  |  Overly complex: fact 3, fact 4  |  Missing orientation: fact 5, fact 6, fact 8

options.label: Fact 1 · Menu entries named after software modules
options.why: Functions instead of benefits. The menu speaks in the software's terms, not in what the learner wants to do: functions instead of benefits.

options.label: Fact 2 · Button “Enrol in module instance”
options.why: Functions instead of benefits. The label names a system object, not the learner's action: functions instead of benefits.

options.label: Fact 3 · 22 entries, 9 widgets and 4 banners at once
options.why: Overly complex. Many choices at once before any action: overly complex.

options.label: Fact 4 · 14 filters before any result
options.why: Overly complex. Fourteen decisions before a result: overly complex.

options.label: Fact 5 · The same lesson in three lists, three orders
options.why: Missing orientation. The learner cannot tell where the lesson is or which list counts: missing orientation.

options.label: Fact 6 · No “Continue where you stopped”
options.why: Missing orientation. Nothing tells the learner what to do next: missing orientation.

options.label: Fact 7 · A feature added last year, opened by 2%
options.why: Functions instead of benefits. A feature added because the software could do it, not for a learner task: functions instead of benefits.

options.label: Fact 8 · Title and path both read “Home”
options.why: Missing orientation. The learner cannot tell where they are: missing orientation.

sortKey.teachingNote: The sort is objective: one fact belongs to the mistake it breaks first. Two edges: fact 7 (a social feed opened by 2%) is Functions instead of benefits, not Overly complex, although it adds to the clutter: it was added because the software could, not for a learner task. Fact 5 (the same lesson in three lists) is Missing orientation, not complexity: the learner cannot tell which list counts. The goal field, the most frustrating fact and the three expectations are judged: any fact defends if the reason is written from the learner's side (what I expected, what I saw). Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, put yourself in the learner's position, describe 5 problems, formulate 3 expectations.

criticalGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · Why that phase is critical
criticalGuide.answer: Usage is critical: her emotion drops from 4 to 2 there, because the lesson does not fit her twenty minutes, and the next thing she does is to close the app and not return.
criticalGuide.example: At LearnLoop the learning phase is critical: Mia's emotion drops there because the unit is long, and after it she stops.
criticalGuide.why: Materi A3: mark a phase as critical where the emotion is lowest or where the person stops, and say what happens to the emotion and what the person does next. Another phase defends if the sentence says so.
lookFor: Names the phase.
Says what happens to the emotion.
Says what the person does next.

decisionOrderGuide.title: 3.2 · Why the first decision goes first (Core)
decisionOrderGuide.answer: Flexible five-minute formats go first: they fix the learner's critical phase and carry the largest segment, so the first figure (the return rate) moves within twenty weeks. Client reporting follows because it keeps the training managers informed, and the research programme runs beside both.
decisionOrderGuide.example: A resume-anywhere format goes first because it fixes the critical phase of the largest group and moves the first figure within twenty weeks; the research programme runs beside it.
decisionOrderGuide.why: The strategy is an order with a reason. A different order defends if the reason is concrete.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one.
Says what it does for the target group.

frustrationsGuide.title: 1.1 · Frustrations and the decision the persona supports (Core)
frustrationsGuide.answer: She could be frustrated at 21:00, tired, when she must first find where she stopped and then meets a 40-minute lesson, so she closes the app. Because of this persona a team could decide to put a resume button on every screen and to cut lessons into pieces of five minutes.
frustrationsGuide.example: At LearnLoop Mia could be frustrated when she opens a lesson on her phone at night and finds a long page with no way to save her place. A team could decide, because of her, to add a save-my-place button.
frustrationsGuide.why: The plan asks for possible frustrations, and the coaching point says a persona is a decision tool. A good answer names a situation and one decision that would change because of the persona (Materi A1, A2).
lookFor: Names a situation, not a verdict.
Names one decision a team could take because of the persona.
Fits the persona's goals and context.

giveUpGuide.title: 3.2 · What you give up and when that segment gets its turn (Core)
giveUpGuide.answer: I give up the simpler teacher workspace (D2) and the exam-preparation mode (D5) for the first two quarters; the teachers get their turn in the third quarter, and I will tell them the date.
giveUpGuide.example: I give up the exam-preparation mode this year; its users get their turn in the third quarter, and I will tell them the date.
giveUpGuide.why: The skill of Level 3: a decision that gives up nothing has not decided. The answer names a segment that waits and when it is revisited (Materi B2, B3).
lookFor: Names a real segment or decision that waits.
Names when it gets its turn.

journeyProblemsGuide.title: 1.2 (Optional) · Four possible problems that lead to the drop-out
journeyProblemsGuide.answer: 1. A lesson needs 40 minutes in one sitting. 2. It cannot be paused and resumed. 3. The reminder arrives when she is at work. 4. She cannot find where she stopped.
journeyProblemsGuide.example: At LearnLoop: 1. The first lesson is long. 2. Nothing says what comes next. 3. The reminder comes at a bad time. 4. There is no sign of progress.
journeyProblemsGuide.why: The plan asks for four possible problems, not the right four. A good list names situations along the path, one per line.
lookFor: Four lines.
Situations, not verdicts.
Spread over the phases.

journeyR2Guide.title: 3.2 · The critical journey of the target group
journeyR2Guide.answer: entry: Signs up and picks her course. / A start page that does not say how long a lesson takes. / An onboarding step that shows the length of each unit. | work: Starts a lesson at 21:00 on her phone. / 40 minutes in one sitting; no pause. / D1: five-minute formats that can be paused anywhere. | progress: Returns after three days and wants to finish. / She cannot see where she stopped or how far she is. / D1 resumes at the exact place; D4 shows her manager the progress.
journeyR2Guide.example: At LearnLoop, for a teacher: set up: builds a course on Sunday, emotion 2, pain: nine tabs, the strategy acts with a shorter editor. Run: waits for messages, emotion 2, pain: cannot see who is stuck, a list of stuck learners.
journeyR2Guide.why: Materi A3 and B2: map the persona through the three phases; where the emotion is lowest the strategy must act, and the last row names where.
lookFor: A persona named.
Emotion rated for each phase.
A pain point and a point of action in each phase.

missingGuide.title: 2.2 · What information you are missing (Core)
missingGuide.answer: I do not know whether learners leave because the lesson is too long or because they cannot find their place. I would interview five learners who stopped and look at where in the lesson they left.
missingGuide.example: I do not know whether learners leave because the lesson is too long or because they cannot find the course. I would interview five who stopped.
missingGuide.why: The plan asks it outright. A good answer names a specific unknown that would change the decision, and a way to find it out.
lookFor: Names a specific unknown, not “more data”.
Says how it could be found out.

orderGuide.title: 2.2 · Why the first priority goes first (Core)
orderGuide.answer: “Where I stopped” goes first: it answers the learner's lowest point, costs the least (€6,000, two weeks) and is done before the larger measures start. Flexible formats follow because they need the longest.
orderGuide.example: At LearnLoop the resume button goes first: it answers the persona's lowest point, costs the least and is done before the larger measures start.
orderGuide.why: A reason for position one: the persona and the pain point it answers, the cost, or what the others depend on. Segmentation helps: name the group you give most weight.
lookFor: Gives a reason for position one, not for the whole set.
Names the group it weighs most.

personaGuide.title: 1.1 · The learner persona (Core)
personaGuide.answer: Anja Weber, 36, a project manager with two children. She wants the certificate to apply for a team-lead role next year (note 2) and to use what she learns in her project next week (note 5). After three days away she does not know where she stopped (note 3), a lesson needs 40 minutes in one sitting and cannot be paused (note 6), and the reminder arrives at 08:00 while she is at work (note 7). She studies after 21:00 for about 20 minutes on her phone (notes 1 and 4). Her employer pays and her manager wants to see progress (note 8). She expects to land on the exact place where she stopped, a lesson she can finish in 20 minutes, and a sign of progress she can show her manager.
personaGuide.example: Mia, 29, a sales assistant. Goal: qualify for a team-lead role (a reason in her life). Problem: after a few days away she loses the thread. Situation: twenty minutes on her phone in the evening, paid by her employer. She expects to land where she stopped. Sources: two interviews and one log analysis.
personaGuide.why: Materi A1: a persona has goals, problems and the context of use, each stated as a situation, not a verdict, and each with a source. A statement without a source is a hypothesis.
lookFor: Goals as reasons in a life, not feature wishes.
Problems as situations, not “the platform is bad”.
A context with time, device and motivation.
Cites note numbers.
A persona, not a list of notes.
pitfalls: A cliché (“tech-savvy, loves apps”).
Mixing the teacher into the learner persona.

problemsGuide.title: 3.1 · The three biggest problems of the target group
problemsGuide.answer: 1. In the learning phase she meets a 40-minute lesson that cannot be paused. 2. After a break she cannot find where she stopped. 3. The reminder arrives at 08:00, when she is at work, so she ignores it.
problemsGuide.example: At LearnLoop, for the teachers: 1. In the set-up phase the upload takes three hours. 2. In the run phase they cannot see who is stuck. 3. In the review phase they must copy a unit by hand.
problemsGuide.why: The plan asks for the three biggest problems of the target group. Each names the situation and the phase of the journey.
lookFor: Three lines.
Each names a phase.
Situations, not verdicts.

reflectGuide.title: 1.3 (Optional) · Coaching reflection
reflectGuide.answer: For the working professional who studies in twenty minutes at night, not for “the learner” in general. The time-poor learner, because she is the largest group, and the organisation that pays decides on renewals through her usage. At the moment she returns after a break: nothing shows where she stopped.
reflectGuide.why: Reflection is never scored. The plan's coaching points: a persona is a decision tool, not a profile; many personas stay ineffective; a journey reveals systemic problems, not single errors. Use the learners' notes as the start of the live discussion.

segPersonaGuide.title: 3.1 · A strategic persona, in one or two sentences
segPersonaGuide.answer: Anja, a project manager, wants to finish the course in twenty-minute evening slots on her phone, but loses her place after a break (S1: 45% of learners, return rate falling). | Markus, a trainer, wants to build courses with little effort, but the editor has nine tabs and uploading takes hours (S3: 120 teachers who supply all content, 4 of 6 say it is too complicated). | Petra, a training manager, wants to show management that staff finish, but only 31% logged in and she formats the report by hand (S4: 60 accounts that decide renewals).
segPersonaGuide.example: At LearnLoop: Sven, a trainer, wants to build a course in an evening but finds the editor too long (the 90 teachers who supply the content, 3 of 5 interviewed agree).
segPersonaGuide.why: Materi B1: a persona is strategic if a decision would change because of it. One or two sentences with the goal, the problem and situation, and the evidence in the segment's facts.
lookFor: A goal and a problem.
Cites the segment's printed facts.
A decision would change because of it.

sharedGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · A pain point that appears for two groups
sharedGuide.answer: Both the learner and the teacher cannot see where someone is: she does not know where she stopped, he does not know who is stuck. That suggests the cause is the missing view of the course path, not two separate screens.
sharedGuide.example: At LearnLoop both the learner and the teacher cannot see where a course stands, one where she stopped and the other which learners are stuck. That suggests a missing course overview as the cause.
sharedGuide.why: Materi A3: look for a pain point that recurs across personas; it points to a systemic cause that one fix can remove.
lookFor: Names a pain point for two groups.
Names a cause in the process, not a single screen.

targetWhyGuide.title: 3.1 · Why this group first (Core)
targetWhyGuide.answer: Time-poor learners go first: they are the largest segment (45%), their return rate is falling, and their usage is what the training managers measure when they decide on renewals, so one fix helps two segments. Teachers and training managers get a smaller fix later.
targetWhyGuide.example: At LearnLoop the teachers go first: they supply all the content, so if they leave the learners have nothing to learn; the learners wait one quarter and get a smaller fix.
targetWhyGuide.why: Materi B1: say which test decided (size, business value, where the journey breaks) and what the other groups get. The largest group is not always the most important.
lookFor: Names the test.
Says what the other groups get.
Uses the printed figures.

teacherGuide.title: 2.1 (Optional) · The teacher persona
teacherGuide.answer: Markus Feld, 44, a freelance trainer who builds courses. He wants to build and run courses with little effort and to reuse a unit in a second course (notes T1, T6). Uploading one unit takes three hours (T1), the editor has nine tabs and he uses two (T2), and he cannot see which learners are stuck (T3). He builds courses on Sunday evening at his desk (T1), unpaid time next to his own work.
teacherGuide.example: At LearnLoop: Sven, 41, a trainer. Goal: build a course quickly. Problem: the editor hides the upload behind four menus. Situation: builds on Sunday at his desk, unpaid time.
teacherGuide.why: Materi A4: the teacher wants to build and run a course with little effort and to see how learners are doing; a different persona from the learner.
lookFor: A teacher's goal, not a learner's.
Cites T-notes.
A context of use.

uncertainGuide.title: 3.2 · The decision under uncertainty: which persona is prioritised (Core)
uncertainGuide.answer: I decide that time-poor learners (S1) are the prioritised persona for the next two quarters. I do not know whether their falling return rate is caused by the lesson length or by the missing place marker, and the personas rest on only 12 interviews. I reverse if the seven-day return rate of S1 is not up eight points after ten weeks, or if the training managers' renewals of S4 show a drop.
uncertainGuide.example: I decide that teachers are prioritised for two quarters. I do not know whether their complaints come from the editor or from slow uploads. I reverse if learner sign-ups fall by 5% by month four.
uncertainGuide.why: The frame of Materi B3: what I decide, what I do not know, what would make me reverse and by when. A checkable reversal condition has a figure and a time.
lookFor: States the decision.
States what is not known.
A reversal condition with a figure and a time.
pitfalls: A reversal condition no one could check (“if it does not work”).

decisionKey.title: Block 3.2 · Three decisions for the strategy
decisionKey.expected: Flexible five-minute learning formats; Client reporting; A persona research programme

options.label: D1 · Flexible five-minute learning formats (€70,000, 20 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it fixes the critical phase of the largest segment (Materi B1).

options.label: D2 · A simpler teacher workspace (€60,000, 22 weeks)
options.why: Defendable: it serves the teachers who supply all content, but at €60,000 and 22 weeks it is a large project for the second segment.

options.label: D3 · An onboarding path by role (€35,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Defendable and cheap for what it covers, but it changes the first steps only; the learners' critical phase is in the learning phase.

options.label: D4 · Client reporting (€30,000, 12 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: it serves the small but critical training managers cheaply (Materi B1, B2).

options.label: D5 · An exam-preparation mode (€55,000, 18 weeks)
options.why: Defendable for exam preparers, but nothing in the evidence says they are the problem (high satisfaction).

options.label: D6 · A persona research programme (€25,000, 52 weeks)
options.why: Reference pick: the data is thin (12 and 6 interviews), so the research programme tests the personas as hypotheses (Materi B3).

options.label: D7 · A redesign of the public marketing site (€40,000, 10 weeks)
options.why: Rejected: €40,000 for a look that serves none of the pain points.

decisionKey.teachingNote: A different set of three defends if the reason is written and it follows from the target group. The budget is a live hint, not a lock (CLAUDE.md #38); a set over the €220,000 limit exports with the amount printed as a fact.

measureKey.title: Block 2.2 · Choose four measures, rate them, name the pain point, order them
measureKey.expected: “Where I stopped”; Flexible learning formats; One clear course structure; A view of stuck learners. Total €45,000 of €45,000, longest 6 weeks of 13.

options.label: M1 · Flexible learning formats
options.why: Reference measure (learners). Effort High by the printed cost €16,000. Reference ratings: user impact High, risk Mid.

options.label: M2 · “Where I stopped”
options.why: Reference measure (learners). Effort Low by the printed cost €6,000. Reference ratings: user impact High, risk Low.

options.label: M3 · A simpler course editor
options.why: Defendable: it answers T2 for the teachers. A learner who takes it instead of the stuck-learners view stays on the teacher side and should say which teacher pain point it answers.

options.label: M4 · A view of stuck learners
options.why: Reference measure (teachers). Effort Mid by the printed cost €12,000. Reference ratings: user impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: M5 · Reusable units
options.why: Defendable and cheap (€9,000): it answers T6. Strong if the learner says how many teachers it reaches.

options.label: M6 · One clear course structure
options.why: Reference measure (both). Effort Mid by the printed cost €11,000. Reference ratings: user impact Mid, risk Low.

options.label: M7 · An automatic monthly report
options.why: Defendable: €7,000 for the training managers, who decide renewals (T5). It is the cheapest way to reach the third group; as one of four it leaves a learner measure out.

options.label: M8 · Badges for all users
options.why: Rejected: €18,000 for badges that answer no pain point in the notes; it is the typical decoration (Materi A5).

options.label: M9 · A new brand look
options.why: Rejected: €25,000 for a new look that touches no pain point of any persona; impact on every persona is Low.

measureKey.teachingNote: The reference four measures cover learners (M1, M2), both groups (M6) and teachers (M4) and cost exactly the case's €45,000 (a Case assumption). The organisations' complaint is answered through learners who finish. Effort is rule-based (under €8,000 Low, up to €15,000 Mid, above High), so the check can flag it; user impact and risk are judgements and are never marked. The pain point each measure answers must name a persona and a phase. A different, well-reasoned choice is acceptable and exports (CLAUDE.md #38): within the budget, over it, another set of four, a different order, all with a stated reason.

segmentKey.title: Block 3.1 · Strategic personas and the target group
segmentKey.expected: Personas: Time-poor learners; Teachers who build courses; Training managers at client companies. Target group: Time-poor learners.

options.label: S1 · Time-poor learners
options.why: Reference persona and target group: the largest segment (45%), its return rate is falling, and its usage is what S4 measures, so one fix serves two segments (Materi B1).

options.label: S2 · Exam preparers
options.why: Defendable as a persona (15%, high satisfaction), but nothing in the notes says its journey breaks; a weak candidate for first.

options.label: S3 · Teachers who build courses
options.why: Reference persona: 120 teachers supply all content, and 4 of 6 say the editor is too complicated; small but critical (Materi B1).

options.label: S4 · Training managers at client companies
options.why: Reference persona: 60 accounts decide renewals; small and business-critical (Materi B1). A defendable target group: it decides the money.

options.label: S5 · Casual browsers
options.why: Rejected as a strategic persona: rarely finish, no payment link; no decision changes because of this group (Materi A2).

segmentKey.teachingNote: S4 is a good alternative target group: the training managers decide renewals, and an answer that picks S4 and says which test decided (business value) and what the learners get instead defends. A target group that is not among the chosen personas is a gap worth a question. Any of the five defends as target group if the reason names the test (size, value, where the journey breaks) and what the others get.

sortKey.title: Block 1.1 · Eight research notes into three persona fields
sortKey.expected: Goal: note 2, note 5  |  Problem or frustration: note 3, note 6, note 7  |  Context of use: note 1, note 4, note 8

options.label: Note 1 · Studies around 21:00 for 20 minutes on a phone
options.why: Context of use. It says when, for how long and on which device: the context of use.

options.label: Note 2 · Needs the certificate for a team-lead role
options.why: Goal. It is a reason in her life, a role she wants to reach: a goal.

options.label: Note 3 · After three days she does not know where she stopped
options.why: Problem or frustration. A situation where something goes wrong: she loses her place. A problem.

options.label: Note 4 · Median session 14 minutes, 71% on a phone
options.why: Context of use. It describes how long and on which device people use the platform: the context of use.

options.label: Note 5 · Wants to use it in her project next week
options.why: Goal. It is what she wants to be able to do: a goal tied to her work.

options.label: Note 6 · A lesson needs 40 minutes in one sitting
options.why: Problem or frustration. A 40-minute lesson against 20 minutes of time: something gets in her way. A problem.

options.label: Note 7 · The reminder arrives at 08:00, at work
options.why: Problem or frustration. The reminder comes when she cannot use it, so she ignores it: something goes wrong. A problem, even though it names a time.

options.label: Note 8 · The employer pays and the manager wants to see progress
options.why: Context of use. It says why she is on the platform (the employer pays and checks): the motivation part of the context of use.

sortKey.teachingNote: The sort is objective: a note goes where its sentence points. Two edges: note 7 (the reminder arrives at 08:00) names a time, but the time is the trouble, so it is a Problem and not Context of use; note 8 (the employer pays, the manager wants progress) could be read as a goal, but it says why she is on the platform and who is watching, so it is Context of use (motivation). The persona and the frustrations are judged: any persona defends if it names a goal as a reason in a life, problems as situations, a context with time and device, and cites the note numbers. Plan: Arbeitsauftrag 1, describe a persona (goals, problems, usage situation), the expectations and possible frustrations.
